cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-1:
Cicero's letters begin in the first volume of Evelyn Shuckburgh's version, in the 1908 printing. Rome's greatest speaker writes to Atticus, to Caesar, and to dear friends. Politics, gossip, wit, and fear flow from his pen in turn.

No letters from the ancient world feel so alive or so frank. Cicero schemes, jokes, grieves, and boasts as the Republic totters. He never meant these pages for the public eye. That candor makes them a rare window on Rome's fall. The set stands as a source that historians mine like no other from the age. New readers will find no better first guide to his world.
cinq-mars-volume-1:
Alfred de Vigny, a French romantic poet turned novelist, built Cinq-Mars on a real conspiracy against Cardinal Richelieu. Volume 1 opens the English edition with critical essays on De Vigny, by French Academy writers. The novel turns to 1639, as Henri de Cinq-Mars leaves home for the court of Louis XIII. Ambition and love launch him toward glory and ruin.

Cinq-Mars rises fast as the king's favorite at a fearful court. He loves Marie de Gonzague, a princess whose rank sits far above his reach. Richelieu, the cardinal who rules France, watches the favorite climb with patience. War with Spain, sieges, and festivals fill the background of the man's ascent. De Thou, his friend and a counsellor's son, walks beside him toward the plot. Readers starting the English set get the setup: a favorite's charm, a minister's power, and a love that ambition will poison by degrees.
conscience-volume-1:
Hector Malot's crime novel begins in Conscience, Volume 1, the first English portion of the French Immortals edition. A life of Malot opens the file: the Norman novelist of Sans Famille, dead in 1907, praised for honest work over fashion. Conscience itself appeared in 1893. The story opens at Crozat's Wednesday reunion of old school comrades, where fortunes made and missed are quietly compared over dinner.

Inside, Saniel steps forward: a poor young doctor from Auvergne, brilliant, starved, and proud. He has begged three thousand francs from Glady, a comrade grown rich, and felt the humiliation to the bone. The moneylender Caffie holds the papers that could crush his start in medicine. Malot sets poverty, pride, and ambition in one room and lets them argue. Readers starting Conscience meet the murderer before the crime, as a man whose conscience is still loud enough to make his fall a tragedy rather than a puzzle.
correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-volum:
Richard Wagner and Franz Liszt, the two giants of romantic music, exchanged the letters gathered in Correspondence of Wagner and Liszt, Volume 1. Francis Hueffer translated the German letters into English. Wagner's own preface tells how Liszt rescued his art when success had failed and exile loomed. At Weimar, Liszt took the conductor's baton and gave the homeless composer a stage.

Letters from the 1840s onward track premieres, money troubles, and plans between the two men. Liszt conducts Tannhauser at Weimar while Wagner watches, hearing his music as if from a second self. Lohengrin, forgotten on paper during Wagner's despair in Paris, sounds at last through Liszt's loyalty. Requests, thanks, creeds, and family news fill the pages between the events. The friendship becomes the plot: one man composing, the other fighting the world's stages open. Readers use the volume as a record of how opera survived its hardest decade.
cosmopolis-volume-1:
Paul Bourget, a French novelist of society and belief, sets Cosmopolis in Rome, where Europe's aristocracies mix in one salon world. Volume 1 introduces the Marquis de Montfanon, a scarred French legitimist turned collector. Montfanon gathers documents for a history of the French nobility and the Church. Rome itself is a museum that everyone raids for relics.

An old socialist bookseller named Ribalta trades epigrams with the marquis across the counter of ideas. Catholic faith and free thought spar politely while sharing old hatreds. Princes, artists, diplomats, and beautiful visitors of many nations crowd the drawing rooms. Love affairs begin under the cover of art talk and antiquarian hunts. Bourget studies each soul like a case: pride, faith, and desire pulling in different tongues. Readers starting Cosmopolis should expect psychology over plot, with Rome's ruins and churches judging the modern chatter around them.
critical-and-historical-essays-volume-1:
Thomas Babington Macaulay made his fame with the Edinburgh Review essays gathered here in volume one of his Critical and Historical Essays. Macaulay's editor lists the pieces with their dates, beginning with Milton in 1825. This volume includes his essays on Hallam's Constitutional History, on Burleigh and his times, on Horace Walpole, and on Warren Hastings, the governor of India later impeached.

Each essay starts from a book under review and gallops off into a full retelling of an age, confident, quotable, and partisan for progress. Macaulay writes history like a speech to a jury, with scenery. Later scholars corrected his details, as his editor admits, but his bird's-eye surveys still give readers a first map of English politics and letters.
curtius-history-greece-vol-1:
Ernst Curtius begins his History of Greece in this first volume, in A. W. Ward's 1867 English version. Land and sea come first, then legend and the Dorian migrations. Curtius, a German scholar who dug at Olympia, grounds myth in soil and coast.

He explains Greece through its harbors, hills, and scattered islands. Tribes move, shrines rise, and the first cities take shape in his telling. Learning and landscape walk hand in hand throughout. The volume opened a history that married the spade to the scroll, and Victorian readers took it as the fullest Greek story of its day.
darwin-descent-of-man-vol-1:
Charles Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, twelve years after his Origin of Species. In the first volume he at last applies his theory of evolution to human beings directly. The first edition text is used here, in the first of two volumes.

Darwin compares the bodies and minds of humans and animals, trait by trait. He argues that the likeness is too deep for separate creation, and that humans descend from earlier forms of life. He also sets out his second great idea, selection in relation to sex, which volume two then takes up in full.
darwin-life-and-letters-vol-1:
Francis Darwin edited his father's Life and Letters in 1887, five years after Charles Darwin's death. Volume One covers the making of the naturalist. It includes Darwin's own short autobiography, written for his family.

Readers follow the young Darwin from Cambridge to the Beagle voyage that changed his life. The barnacle years, his secret work on species, and the shock of Wallace's letter all appear. Letters show his doubts, his care for facts, and his dread of the storm to come. The volume ends as the Origin of Species readies for print in 1859. A chapter of personal recollections by Francis adds a son's close view.
davis-rise-and-fall-vol-1:
Jefferson Davis published the first volume of The Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government in 1881. The former Confederate president wrote to defend secession and his own conduct. Volume One is mostly argument, not battle narrative.

Davis lays out his view that the states kept their sovereignty under the Constitution and could lawfully leave the Union. He traces the slavery dispute and the path to war through that legal lens. Critics charged that he fought the war again on paper. Supporters took the book as their brief. Either way, it is the fullest statement of the Confederate case by its own chief.
demosthenes-public-orations-kennedy-vol-:
Demosthenes' Public Orations gather the great state speeches of Athens' leading orator, in Charles Rann Kennedy's English translation. This first volume spans his career around 330 BC, when Athens stood in the shadow of Macedon. The speeches were working weapons in the assembly and the courts.

Readers meet the speech on the crown, where Demosthenes defends his whole public life against his rival Aeschines. Other speeches weigh treaties, taxes, and the conduct of generals in the field. Together they show how a free city argued about war and honor in the open. The volume is a front-row seat at Athenian democracy under strain.
dialogues-of-the-buddha-vol-1:
The Dialogues of the Buddha are the English form of the Digha Nikaya, the long discourses of the Pali canon. T. W. and Caroline Rhys Davids translated this first volume in 1899. The Digha holds 34 long suttas, talks the Buddha gave across northern India.

The talks take many shapes: debates with Brahmins, answers to wandering ascetics, and sermons to kings and villagers. The first discourse sorts right and wrong views like a net catching fish. Others treat the marks of a great man and the fruits of the homeless life. Rhys Davids' notes place each talk in its world. The volume opens the most readable shelf of the Pali canon.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-1:
George Meredith opens Diana of the Crossways in this first volume, chapters one to eight. A chapter on diaries and diarists introduces Diana, whose private notebooks frame the tale. An Irish ball in Dublin shows her beauty and spirit in triumph. Mr. Redworth's interior and Mr. Sullivan Smith's exterior are sketched in contrast.

Hints of Diana's experiences explain her flight from a husband and a name. Her brilliance draws admirers, gossips, and danger in London. The crisis of the volume brings her to the crossways of reputation and freedom. Meredith writes his heroine as a new kind of woman: intellectual, imprudent, and loyal. This opening portion sets up her friendship with Emma, her fame as a talker, and the world's readiness to misjudge her.
dickinson-letters-vol-1:
Mabel Loomis Todd edited the first volume of Emily Dickinson's letters in 1894, four years after the poet's death. Dickinson had lived in near seclusion in Amherst, yet her letters blazed with wit and feeling. Volume One opens the correspondence of her early and middle years.

She writes to friends, cousins, and her sister-in-law Sue about books, gardens, faith, and death. Many letters carry poems slipped in like gifts. Her compressed, electric style in prose matches the poems that made her famous. Readers who know only the verse will find the other half of her genius in these pages.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-1:
Dio Cassius, a Roman senator from Bithynia, wrote an eighty-book history of Rome from Aeneas to his own day, around 230 CE. Earnest Cary translated it for the Loeb series between 1914 and 1927. The first volume holds what survives of books one through eleven, from the founding of Rome to the Punic wars.

These early books come down only in fragments, saved by Byzantine readers who copied out choice passages. Even so, Dio gives the broadest single story of the rise of Rome. Readers start here for the kings, the young republic, and the first great wars with Carthage. His later books carry the tale to the emperors.
diodorus-library-booth-vol-1:
Sicilian historian Diodorus compiled a universal Library of History in the last century before Christ. George Booth translated it into English long ago. Volume One holds Books One through Five.

Diodorus opens with Egypt, its gods, kings, and customs. Assyria, Ethiopia, and Arabia follow in his world tour. Greek myth fills the later books of this set. He preserves tales and facts from writers now lost. His style is plain and his net is wide. Readers get a one-man encyclopedia of the ancient world as Rome first knew it. Booth's old English adds period charm throughout.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek teacher living in Rome, wrote his Roman Antiquities around 7 BCE to show Greeks that Rome rose by merit. Edward Spelman's English version of 1758 opens with books one and two. They treat the deep past of Italy before the city had kings of its own line.

Aeneas lands in Italy, Romulus founds the city, and the first kings build its rites and laws. Dionysius gives long speeches and digs into points that Livy passes fast. His work is our fullest source for the regal age of Rome. The Greek text aims to praise Rome while it tells her myths straight.

donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-v:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, Volume 1, by Gilbert Parker, opens his Egyptian story cycle. Parker's contents for this volume list four tales. While the Lamp Holds Out to Burn leads. The Price of the Grindstone and the Desertion of Mahommed Selimon follow. The Reef of Norman's Woe closes the set. His introduction calls the book a herald. The novel The Weavers was to come after it.

The Donovan of the title is Dicky Donovan. Parker makes him a small, shrewd English official in Cairo. He understands Egyptians as few Englishmen bother to do. Around him move soldiers, priests, peasants, and pashas. Each tale tests British rule at ground level. A grindstone's price or a soldier's desertion can expose the whole system. Parker served his Egypt in imagination thoroughly. He writes occupation as a web of personal debts, favors, and revenge.
droll-stories-volume-1:
Honore de Balzac's Droll Stories, first published in 1832, collect tales he claimed came from the abbeys of Touraine, written in a Rabelaisian vein. This first volume holds the first ten tales plus prologue and epilogue. The Fair Imperia opens the set at the Council of Constance, where courtesans and cardinals trade favors.

The Venial Sin spins a whole tale-cycle from one adultery: how the child was procured, repented, and mourned. The King's Sweetheart, The Devil's Heir, and the merrie jests of Louis the Eleventh fill out the volume. A wife demanding whether friends are usually kept in chests shows the dialogue's snap. Balzac's contemporaries were shocked and delighted in equal measure.
dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life-volu: Dynevor Terrace, or The Clue of Life, volume one, by Charlotte Yonge. The Welsh family's tale begins. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
embers-volume-1:
Embers, Volume 1, by Gilbert Parker, collects the songs and poems of a novelist better known for prose. Parker's contents list twenty one pieces in this first volume. The title poem Embers leads. Rosleen, Will You Come Back Home, and Mary Callaghan and Me follow. Irish names and Irish longings run through the early pages. Kildare and Farcalladen Rise keep the company.

Other pieces turn seaward and outward. At Sea, Eyes Like the Sea, and Under the Cliff stand beside I Heard the Desert Calling. Parker wrote verse all his life alongside the Pierre tales and the Egyptian stories. These are songs first, meant for music and recitation. Exile is their great subject. The singer is always somewhere else: on the sea, in the desert, in London. Home is the place the voice is coming from, or the place it cannot reach again.
essays-political-economical-and-philosop:
Benjamin Thompson, known as Count Rumford, gathered his practical essays in this first volume, covering poor relief, food, and fireplaces. Rumford, an American-born scientist working in Bavaria for the Elector Palatine, described the establishment for the poor he ran at Munich. Beggars were housed, fed, and set to work, and Rumford reported the costs and results in detail.

Further essays lay out principles for poor relief in any country, cheap nourishing food for the poor, and chimney fireplaces redesigned to save fuel and stop smoke. A fifth essay surveys other Bavarian public institutions. Everything is measured, priced, and tested: Rumford wrote social reform like an engineer, with soup and chimneys as his machines.
ethics-part-1:
Benedict de Spinoza opens his Ethics, here in R H M Elwes's translation, with part one, Concerning God, written in geometric order. Definitions come first: self-caused, finite, substance, attribute, and mode, each stated in a sentence or two. From these he builds propositions proving that God, an infinite substance, necessarily exists.

Spinoza concludes that God and all God's attributes are unchangeable, and that nothing could be other than it is, since all follows from the divine nature. Mind and body, he argues, do not act on each other, being one substance under two attributes. This first part lays the foundation stone of his whole system, and its austere definitions still reward slow reading.
euclid-elements-heath-vol-1:
Thomas L. Heath published his definitive translation of Euclid's Elements in 1908. Volume one covers Books One through Four of the thirteen. Euclid had assembled the Elements around 300 BCE in Alexandria.

Geometry here builds from a handful of definitions, postulates, and common notions. Triangles, parallels, and circles receive rigorous step-by-step proof. The Pythagorean theorem arrives as the forty-seventh proposition of Book One. Heath's introduction and notes explain two thousand years of commentary. The Elements became the most influential mathematics textbook in history. Schoolchildren learned logic itself from Euclid's order for centuries. Heath's edition remains the standard English Euclid for scholars.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-1:
Arthur S. Way translated the whole of Euripides into English verse for the Loeb series, first printed in 1912. Volume one holds five plays: Iphigenia at Aulis, Rhesus, Hecuba, The Daughters of Troy, and Helen. The scan staged here is a 1930 reprint of that edition.

Iphigenia faces sacrifice so the Greek fleet may sail, while Hecuba and the Trojan women count war's cost. Helen offers a startling twist: the real Helen never went to Troy at all. Way chose verse where other translators used prose, keeping song in the choruses. His set was the only complete English verse Euripides of its time. The library also holds Murray's versions of single plays.
euripides-tragedies-buckley-vol-1:
T. A. Buckley translated ten tragedies of Euripides in this first volume, in literal prose. The set includes Hecuba, Orestes, Medea, Hippolytus, and both Iphigenia plays. Buckley's versions served Victorian readers who wanted accuracy over poetry.

Euripides was the most questioning of the three great Athenian tragedians. His gods behave badly, his heroes argue like lawyers, and his women speak memorably. Buckley's plain prose lets students follow plots and speeches exactly. The style can feel dated beside verse translations like Murray's. For checking what the Greek actually says, generations of readers trusted this workmanlike volume.
evan-harrington-volume-1:
George Meredith's novel Evan Harrington begins in this first volume with a death in a tailor's shop. Melchisedec Harrington, the great Mel, dies at Lymport-on-the-Sea, leaving a widow and gifted children. His son Evan inherits skill, pride, and a trade the world calls low. His daughters, the daughters of the shears, aim far higher.

Chapters follow Evan on board the Jocasta and on the road as a gentleman traveller. His sister the Countess de Saldar schemes to launch him in grand society. His mother, stately and unrelenting, presses the family's claims. Meredith sets the book's ruling conflict early: Evan loves the work of his hands yet longs for rank. This opening volume covers chapters one to seven of a comedy about class shame and ambition.
evliya-travels-hammer-vol-1:
Evliya Celebi wandered the Ottoman world for forty years, and Joseph von Hammer's 1834 English selections open his vast travel book. Constantinople, the Balkans, and the road east fill this first volume. No city, dish, or custom escapes his hungry curiosity.

Evliya served sultans, joined campaigns, and collected marvels at every stop. His ten volumes form the greatest travel work of the Islamic world. Fact and tall tale mix freely, to the reader's delight. Von Hammer's selections first brought this inexhaustible guide to English readers, who met in him a companion both learned and endlessly entertaining.
evolution-of-expression-volume-1:
Charles Wesley Emerson's Evolution of Expression, volume one, trains students of oratory through chosen literature. Emerson founded the Emerson College of Oratory in Boston. This thirty-third edition compiles selections illustrating the first stages of his system. Animation, analysis, and smoothness head his method's key.

Dickens's tea-kettle and cricket open the readings, with Browning's Pied Piper beside them. Lyrics by Tennyson, Ingelow, and Ruskin build the first chapter's ladder. Goldsmith's village preacher and the twenty-third Psalm anchor the second. Stevenson's child verse gives young speakers their models. Later chapters rise to Spartacus addressing the gladiators and Emerson on self-reliance. Shakespeare's Hamlet instructing the players closes the volume's selections. The book is a working recitation anthology, arranged so that feeling, voice, and gesture grow together by graded practice.
faust-part-1:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe spent decades on this drama of the scholar who bargains with the devil, and Part 1 is the portion the world knows best. This English verse edition carries a long introduction before the play. It gives a life of Goethe, from Wetzlar and Weimar to his death in 1832, and an account of the older Faust legend he inherited. A prologue for the theatre and a prologue in heaven precede the action.

Faust, sick of learning, summons spirits and signs with Mephistopheles for experience without limit. The price comes due in the Gretchen story, which the introduction notes was Goethe's own development of the tale. A village girl is courted, ruined, and destroyed while heaven and hell dispute her soul. The edition prints no translator's name in its front matter.

following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 1, by Mark Twain, launches his journey around the world from Hartford, Connecticut. Twain inscribes the book to Harry Rogers, a young friend, teasing him about what he is and what he may become unless he models himself on the author. The joke dedication sets the tone: affection delivered as a warning label.

Part 1 also prints the Pudd'nhead maxims, calendar sayings Twain says he gathered from observation, not practice, since teaching goodness is nobler work and costs nothing. The opening chapters then take ship and start westward across the Pacific by way of Hawaii, in diary form. Twain had gone around the world lecturing to pay off his debts, and the voyage became this book: part travel diary, part comic essay, part report on the British Empire's far edges.
frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-musician-v:
Frederick Niecks published the first volume of Frederick Chopin, as a Man and Musician in 1888, reaching a third edition in 1902. Niecks states his method in the preface: facts first, conclusions after. The biographer's compromise between the desirable and the necessary governs his pages. A proem on Poland and the Poles sets the scene.

Nineteen chapters follow Chopin's Polish childhood, his Warsaw schooling, and his departure for the west. Niecks collected letters, recollections, and documents with German patience. He discusses Liszt's earlier life of Chopin, exuberant in style but full of good things. The volume ends before the great Paris years are done. Niecks writes the first scholarly Chopin biography, dry where Liszt rhapsodized. Musicians still mine it for the evidence he gathered at first hand.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-1:
Edward Freeman opens his vast History of the Norman Conquest in this first volume, from 1867. Edward the Confessor's reign sows the seeds of crisis. Harold, William, and a disputed succession take shape as the storm gathers over England.

Freeman rebuilt the tale of 1066 from the sources with huge labor. He weighs charters, chronicles, and claims like a judge in court. His love for the old English cause burns through the learning. The volume began a work of staggering scale, one that set the fullest account of the Conquest before the English-reading world for generations.
freytag-soll-und-haben-bd-1:
Gustav Freytag's Soll und Haben, given here in German, begins the tale of Anton Wohlfart in its first volume. Young Anton enters a merchant house and learns the trade from the desk up. Debit and credit, the twin heads of the ledger, become a school for life.

Anton's rise tests his honesty against greed, ease, and bad company. Freytag builds the counting house into a full moral world. Work, thrift, and plain dealing form the hero's creed. The novel founded German bourgeois realism, and German readers still meet it as a mirror of the middle class that made modern Germany.
froissart-chronicles-johnes-vol-1:
Jean Froissart, a French priest and courtier, spent his life gathering the deeds of the Hundred Years' War into his Chronicles. Thomas Johnes's English translation, in the 1844 Smith edition, fills two volumes. This first volume covers the war from its beginnings to about 1385.

Froissart rides from court to court, questioning knights who fought at Crécy and Poitiers, and writes war as a pageant of honor. Sieges, ransoms, single combats, and the Black Prince's campaigns fill his pages. He favors no nation, only brave deeds well told. The Chronicles are the great picture of chivalry in its last age, drawn by a man who loved it.
from-the-easy-chair-volume-1:
George William Curtis's From the Easy Chair, Volume One, gathers his Tatler-like essays on matters that occurred to him from time to time. Curtis takes his motto from The Tatler itself: to report and weigh whatever matters come to mind.

Contents include Edward Everett in 1862, Dickens reading in 1867, Emerson lecturing, shops and shopping, Mrs. Grundy and the cosmopolitan, and Thalberg and other pianists. Later pieces treat Wendell Phillips at Harvard, Easter bonnets, Jenny Lind, a little dinner with Thackeray, and Robert Browning in Florence. Readers who enjoy urbane American essays will find Curtis civilised, witty and wide-ranging.
fromont-and-risler-volume-1:
Alphonse Daudet's factory novel begins in Fromont and Risler, Volume 1, behind a critical life of Daudet. The essay contrasts him with Zola: Daudet spontaneous, Zola methodical. Born at Nimes in 1840, Daudet suffered as a school usher before Paris and Lettres de mon Moulin made his name. The novel turns to the Fromont wallpaper house.

Risler the elder, a Swiss engineer, brings his talent and honesty into the Paris firm. Georges Fromont, the heir, prefers pleasure to ledgers and leaves work to his partner. Little Sidonie Chebe, from the shop across the way, watches the great house with hungry eyes. Her brother Desire and the cashier Sigismond mark the firm's loyal side. Daudet sets his pieces with speed: factory, shop, and parlor in a few streets. Readers starting the volumes meet the triangle early: a tireless husband, a careless partner, and a girl who means to climb by marriage.
froude-english-ireland-vol-1:
Penal laws open the first volume of Froude's English in Ireland, from 1872. A Protestant few rule a Catholic many in eighteenth-century Ireland. Froude feels Ireland's pain, yet stands by the Union with England throughout.

His telling stirred angry debate on every side at its first appearance. Harsh statutes, absentee landlords, and sullen poverty fill his chapters. He writes with vigor, sympathy, and stubborn conviction at once. The volume began a history that remains fiercely argued over. It is a vivid record of a sad century, by a writer whose strong views add lasting interest.
froude-history-england-vol-1:
James Anthony Froude opens his great Tudor history with the fall of Cardinal Wolsey, in this first volume from 1858. A crisis over the king's marriage gathers force at court. Behind it looms the larger storm of the English Reformation.

Froude drew on state papers that few had used before him. He retold the Tudor age as high drama, with vivid scenes and strong verdicts. Critics charged him with haste and bias, yet readers devoured the books. The opening volume made the fifteen hundreds come alive for the Victorian public, and it still sets the tone for his whole bold enterprise.

An editorial note opens the record of the President's trip in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It is the unnumbered item before document 710, describing the trip log from which the next document is drawn. The log covers July 6 to August 7, 1945.

The note explains that Lieutenant William Rigdon, the President's personal secretary on the trip, compiled the log. It lists the compiled document's eleven parts in order. They run from a table of contents and a foreword by Lieutenant Elsey to a summary itinerary and the party list. The body of the log itself runs to 53 pages, followed by an appendix on the cruiser Augusta. Texts of the Japan surrender proclamation and the conference report are included. A roster of the military police who guarded the Little White House at Babelsberg closes the list, with photographs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-1:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 16, 1945, record the U.S. military team's first Potsdam session. The extracts, taken at 10 a.m., are an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. The subject was how to run the military side of the conference, code-named Terminal.

Admiral Leahy said the staff paper before them assumed the Russians would take the initiative. Moscow, in that view, should bring up the subjects it wished to discuss with the U.S. chiefs. General Marshall added that the U.S. side had subjects of its own and was not so restricted. Admiral King warned against promising to finish work with the British first. Talks with the Russians might have to cut across the combined meetings. The chiefs approved the secretaries' plan for meeting arrangements and attendance, and a memo for the President.

The note keeps the volume's chain of evidence intact.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d832a-1: This editorial note follows document 832 in the second Potsdam volume, near the end of the main run of papers. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d844a-1: This editorial note follows document 844 in the second Potsdam volume. The note keeps the Bucharest thread easy to trace.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d976a-1: Editors of the Foreign Relations volume placed this short note right after document 976. It adds no new material of its own. Instead, it directs readers who want the final word on reparations from Germany to the closing texts of the Potsdam Conference. Those texts, the Protocol and the Communiqué, appear later in the volume. The note gives their page numbers as 1485 and 1505. Such notes help readers jump from the working papers to the settled agreement.
gao-gaoreports-b-299131-1: Operational Research Consultants doubled its February 2007 protest — two case numbers, one consulting fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gellius-attic-nights-rolfe-loeb-vol-1:
Aulus Gellius, a Roman judge and book lover of the second century, spent winter nights in Athens jotting down what he read and heard. His Attic Nights grew into twenty books of notes on words, laws, tales, and old customs. John C. Rolfe translated the work for the Loeb series, and this volume holds books one through five.

One page fixes the true sense of a Latin word, and the next tells a tale of a Roman hero or a Greek wit. Gellius quotes scores of books that are now lost, and so keeps their lines alive. The miscellany charms because it follows one curious mind. Teachers and writers mined it for centuries.
gerfaut-volume-1:
Charles de Bernard, a pupil of Balzac, opens Gerfaut with a critical life of himself. Volume 1 reprints the essay: Bernard dead at forty-eight in 1850, Gerfaut of 1838 judged his greatest work. Its story, the essay says, hangs on a married woman's love for the hero. Sketches of Marillac and Mademoiselle de Corandeuil win praise.

The novel carries a traveler toward the castle of Baron de Bergenheim. A dismissed carpenter, Lambernier, curses the baron beside the road and vows revenge. The stranger studies the lonely chateau as if stone might turn to glass. Bernard builds unease from small signs in these chapters. Rank and wounded pride already press on the household. Readers starting Gerfaut should expect Balzac's world in a lighter style: a country house, a watched wife, and a guest whose curiosity is not about architecture.
godwin-political-justice-1793-vol-1:
William Godwin published An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice in 1793, in the heat of the French Revolution's first years. Volume one opens his vast argument against government itself. Godwin holds that reason, left free, can guide people without coercion. Truth, calmly shown, will in time win every honest mind.

From that faith he attacks laws, courts, and rulers as crutches for a young species. Private judgment, not obedience, is his moral center. The work is the first systematic statement of philosophical anarchism. It made Godwin famous across Britain at once. Volume one lays the theory's base. Its calm confidence still surprises readers.
goethe-wilhelm-meister-carlyle-1824-vol-:
Thomas Carlyle's translation of Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship and Travels appeared in 1824, and Volume 1 began the story. Goethe's novel, Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship, was a classic in Germany but little known in Britain. Carlyle, a young Scottish writer, made it his first big work.

Wilhelm, a merchant's son, leaves trade for the theater and travels with actors, nobles, and wanderers. Each encounter shapes his slow growth toward a settled view of life. The novel, called a Bildungsroman, made the hero's inner formation the plot itself. Carlyle's version introduced German literature to Britain and changed what English readers expected a novel could do.
govdocs-archive_org-majestic-12-official:
Majestic 12 is the name given to an alleged secret committee, supposedly set up under President Truman to handle crashed UFOs and their occupants. This file is the FBI's own record on the matter, file 65-81170, twenty-two pages of declassified documents.

The Bureau collected the famous Eisenhower briefing papers and the inquiries about them, and its agents noted their doubts on the documents themselves; the FBI judged the briefing paper a fake. Readers can inspect the file the Bureau actually kept, rather than later retellings. For the Majestic 12 debate, this is the primary official record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenMarkSuitHo:
James Hosty was the Dallas FBI agent assigned to Lee Harvey Oswald in 1963, and his handling of the case became a scandal after the assassination. Researcher Mark Allen sued for Hosty's records, and this batch holds what the Bureau released in that suit.

The records come from the FBI's communications section and date to February 1977, as the House Select Committee was reopening the assassination inquiry. The batch is numbered 212-13-84 in the release sequence. Files like these are the yield of FOIA litigation: documents the Bureau gave up only because a citizen went to court for them.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIReportCD-1_F:
Commission Document 1 is a letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover to J. Lee Rankin, general counsel of the Warren Commission. Hoover writes about FBI liaison with the commission that was investigating President Kennedy's death. Among the arrangements was a direct wire between the Bureau's New York office and Washington.

As the first numbered document, the letter sets the working terms between the two bodies. The commission depended on the FBI for evidence, so the liaison lines mattered. Hoover's letter shows the machinery being connected, at the start of an inquiry that would run on Bureau files.
govdocs-archive_org-tzsches-will-to-powe:
Friedrich Nietzsche never published The Will to Power himself. Volume 1 gathers notes he left behind in his notebooks, assembled after his collapse and death by his sister and her editors.

The notes circle his great late themes: the will to power as the drive beneath all values, and the revaluation of all values he believed Europe needed to survive its own decay. Because editors chose and ordered the fragments, scholars still argue over what Nietzsche himself would have kept or burned. Even so, the volume is a cornerstone of Nietzsche studies. It shows a restless philosopher thinking on paper, before the arguments hardened into finished books.
govdocs-archive_org-ufo1_20240815_UFO_de: UFO made public docs 1: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-untitled-document-1: Belinda Sue Winchester kept a timeline of what she describes as targeting and harassment directed at her. The document is her own log, set down in her own order and words. The library keeps it as an archive item and takes no stance on her claims. Personal timelines like this one record how a person experienced a long grievance. Readers meet an unfiltered first-person account, preserved as she wrote it.
gregory-tours-history-franks-dalton-vol-:
Gregory, bishop of Tours, completed his History of the Franks in 594, the foundational narrative of Merovingian Gaul. O. M. Dalton's 1927 Clarendon translation is the text here, in its first volume. Gregory wrote as a participant: a Gallo-Roman bishop among Frankish kings he knew and feared.

The first books run from the creation to the death of Clovis, founder of the Frankish kingdom. Then the story thickens into Gregory's own world of warring grandsons, queens at feud, and bishops in peril. Miracles crowd beside murders, both reported in the same plain tone. Without Gregory, the sixth century in Gaul would be nearly dark. His history is vivid, gossipy, and priceless.
haeckel-evolution-of-man-vol-1:
Ernst Haeckel, Germany's great champion of Darwin, published The Evolution of Man in 1874 as Anthropogenie. This first volume treats human embryology and his biogenetic law: the idea that an animal's growth in the egg replays its race's long descent. After Darwin's own books, it was the most widely read popular evolution text of the century.

Haeckel traces man's development through the vertebrate series, stage by stage and plate by plate. His famous embryo drawings argue the case in pictures. The science is bold, sweeping, and in places wrong, as later critics showed. The volume is a landmark of nineteenth-century popular science all the same.
haeckel-history-of-creation-vol-1:
Ernst Haeckel's History of Creation, first issued in German in 1868, was the book that made Darwinism a mass movement in Germany. Volume one sets out the general doctrine: evolution as the key to all nature. Haeckel lectured the material at Jena before publishing it.

He treats spontaneous generation, the rise of life from simple cells, and the single branching tree of all living things. Darwin's theory is preached here as a worldview, not a hypothesis. The style is combative and grand, aimed at general readers rather than professors. Later editions ran for decades. The volume is a founding text of popular evolution in Europe.
haeckel-the-wonders-of-life-a-popular-st: The Wonders of Life, a popular study of biological philosophy, Haeckel's work. Life's wonders. This book preserves that book. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
hafez-divan-clarke-1891-vol-1:
Hafez of Shiraz, who died in 1390, is the most loved lyric poet of Persia, and his Divan is the book Persians keep beside the Quran. H. Wilberforce Clarke gave the first complete English Divan in 1891, in prose, and this is its first volume. His edition carries a preface on Sufism and a life of the poet.

The ghazals sing of wine, the tavern, and the beloved's curls. The nightingale and the rose fill their lines. Persians read them as both love song and scripture of the spirit. Clarke's notes explain every hard name and image. His learning is vast and his apparatus heavy, yet the poems shine through. No other English version of his age took in the whole Divan.
haft-paikar-wilson-1924-vol-1:
C. E. Wilson gave English its first complete Haft Paikar in 1924, and Volume I holds the translation. Nizami's Persian romance follows King Bahram Gur, who finds the portraits of seven princesses and weds them all. Each princess, housed in her own colored dome, tells the king a tale on her appointed night.

The seven tales, framed by the king's hunts and wars, form the crown of Persian romantic epic. Probsthain's Oriental Series issued Wilson's version, a labor of exact scholarship. Volume I lets English readers walk the full shining structure as Nizami built it in the twelfth century.
hallam-constitutional-history-vol-1:
Henry Hallam traces England's constitution from Henry the Seventh to Charles the First in this first volume, from 1827. Parliament's long struggle with the crown forms his central thread. Hallam, a Whig, reads the past as the slow growth of legal liberty.

He weighs statutes, cases, and speeches with a lawyer's precision. Tudor strength and Stuart claims collide in his calm, firm prose. Every Victorian statesman of note read and cited his judgments. The work founded a school of constitutional history in English. Its first volume shows how law, not mere force, became the frame of English freedom.
hallam-middle-ages-vol-1:
Medieval Europe spreads out in the first volume of Hallam's View of the State of Europe, in the 1878 printing. Feudal custom, the Church's vast power, and Italy's free republics fill his survey. Hallam was among the first in English to treat the Middle Ages as a serious, ordered age.

Before him, many called those centuries a mere dark age. After him, they formed a field of study in their own right. His comparative eye ranges from manor to monastery to city state. The book helped invent medieval studies for English readers, and its calm, wide learning still earns it a place on the shelf.
hawkesworth-account-voyages-southern-hem:
John Hawkesworth, a London writer, was hired by the Admiralty to shape the Pacific voyages into an official account. His Account of the Voyages came out in 1773 in three volumes. This first volume sets the scene and carries Captain Cook's first voyage, in the Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, toward its start.

Hawkesworth wove the journals of Cook and Joseph Banks into one smooth narrative voice. The voyage's work was double: watch the transit of Venus from Tahiti, then hunt for a southern continent. Readers of 1773 met Tahitian society in these pages with a shock of delight and scandal. The book was a bestseller and a lightning rod.
heath-history-greek-mathematics-vol-1:
Thomas L. Heath published his History of Greek Mathematics in 1921 in two volumes. Volume one runs from Thales to Euclid across three centuries. Heath was himself the great English translator of Euclid and Archimedes.

The story begins with Thales' first theorems and Egyptian measures. Pythagoras, Plato's circle, and Eudoxus extend geometry step by step. Heath explains how the Greeks invented rigorous proof itself. He writes from total command of the original Greek sources. The volume stands as the standard scholarly history of its subject. Readers watch reason learning to walk, proposition by proposition. Heath's clarity makes even technical passages approachable for general readers.
herodotus-histories-macaulay-vol-1:
Herodotus, the Greek father of history, wrote his Histories in the fifth century before Christ. George Macaulay translated them into clear English prose. Volume One holds Books One through Four.

Herodotus traces the rise of Persia and its clash with Greece. He mixes war reports with tales of kings, customs, and wonders. Egypt, Scythia, and Lydia all get long, curious tours. His method blends inquiry with story in a way no one had tried. The volume opens a classic that still rewards slow reading, half chronicle and half travel book.
hippocrates-genuine-works-adams-vol-1:
Francis Adams translated the Genuine Works of Hippocrates, and volume one holds the core texts. The Hippocratic corpus gathers Greek medical writings from around 400 BCE. The Oath, the Epidemics, and works on prognosis stand in this volume.

Case notes in the Epidemics record illnesses day by day with honesty. Prognostics teaches doctors to foresee a disease's course from signs. Reason takes the place of magic at the bedside throughout. Adams, a Scottish surgeon, translated from the Greek with a practitioner's eye. These are the founding documents of rational medicine in the West. Doctors still swear versions of the Hippocratic Oath today.
historia-augusta-magie-vol-1:
The Historia Augusta claims to be the work of six authors, but most scholars think one hand wrote it around 400 CE. David Magie's Loeb translation of 1921 opens the set. This first volume gives the lives from Hadrian to Alexander Severus, with an index.

Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, and Septimius Severus all get full lives, with lesser men between them. The tone is gossipy: court tales, fake letters, omens, and jokes sit beside sound fact. For the emperors of Rome's crisis age it is often the fullest source there is. Readers must sift it, but they cannot skip it.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's first volume of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, with notes by the Reverend H H Milman, opens the most famous history in English. After the editor's and author's prefaces, chapter one measures the empire's extent and military force in the age of the Antonines. Chapter two praises that age's union and internal prosperity.

The volume runs from the second century through the rise of Christianity and Constantine's conversion, in fifteen chapters. Gibbon weighs emperors, armies, provinces, and the new faith with cool irony, as the middle chapters on northern peoples and Odin's Asgard show. Readers meet his unmatched period style here, balanced sentences carrying a whole civilization toward its long decline.
hobhouse-morals-evolution-1906-vol-1:
Part one of Hobhouse's Morals in Evolution appeared in 1906 as a study in comparative ethics. Hobhouse asks how moral ideas grew from early human groups to civilized society. He gathers customs on family, justice, and the treatment of outsiders. The evidence ranges across peoples and ages.

Custom hardens into moral rule, and rule slowly bends toward wider fairness, in his telling. He tests the story against the thought of his day, including Darwinian accounts. Part one covers the long rise toward civilized morality. A second part takes up the higher morality and the modern state. The pair formed a landmark of early sociology. Its scope still impresses.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-1:
Alexander von Humboldt's Cosmos, in E. C. Otté's English translation for Bohn in 1849, was his last great work: a sketch of a physical description of the whole universe. Volume one lays the frame. Humboldt, in his seventies, aimed to hold all of nature in one view.

He begins with the heavens: nebulae, stars, and the solar system, then descends to Earth itself. The planet's shape, heat, magnetism, volcanoes, and the spread of plants and animals each take their place. The famous introduction argues that nature is one connected whole, felt as much as measured. Cosmos sold hugely and shaped how the Victorian age pictured science.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Alexander von Humboldt traveled South America from 1799 to 1804 with the botanist Aimé Bonpland. His Personal Narrative of that expedition, in Helen Maria Williams's English translation, began appearing in 1814. This first of seven volumes covers the voyage out and the first mainland stages in Venezuela.

Humboldt measures everything: heat, height, magnetism, plants, and stars. He climbs toward Chimborazo's world, collects thousands of new plants, and maps rivers no European had traced. Williams's translation, the first and classic one, carried his mix of science and wonder to English readers. The Narrative made Humboldt the most famous scientist in Europe.
huxley-life-and-letters-vol-1:
Leonard Huxley edited his father's life and letters in 1900, and Volume One covers the rise of Thomas Henry Huxley. Huxley the elder was Darwin's most famous defender. His letters show the fight for evolution from inside.

The young Huxley sails as a ship's surgeon, studies sea life, and wins a place in science. Then come the Darwin years: debates, essays, and the coinage of the word agnostic. Leonard weaves letters with short links of family narrative. The volume gives Victorian science a human face: witty, combative, and warm at home. Friends like Darwin and Tyndall appear throughout the correspondence.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-1:
William Archer's English edition of Henrik Ibsen opened the Norwegian playwright to the English-speaking world, and its first volume gathers three early plays. Lady Inger of Ostrat, The Feast at Solhoug, and Love's Comedy appear in this 1908 collection. History and verse satire dominate the young dramatist's work here.

Medieval legend gives Ibsen his settings: a widow scheming for her son's crown, a wedding feast turned dangerous. Love's Comedy then turns his wit on modern courtship and marriage. Readers watch a genius finding his voice before the famous prose masterpieces arrive. The volume is essential for tracing how the father of modern drama developed. Even the juvenilia carry flashes of the later thunder.
idrisi-geographie-jaubert-vol-1:
Al-Idrisi mapped the known world for Roger the Second of Sicily in 1154, and Jaubert's 1836 French version opens with this first tome. Spain to China passes in review, land by land and sea by sea. An Arab scholar at a Norman court produced the age's greatest geography.

He drew on travelers, merchants, and old books for his vast survey. Climates, cities, products, and marvels fill its ordered chapters. Christian and Muslim learning met in his work at Palermo. The book stands as medieval science at its peak, and Jaubert's translation made it a classic for French readers of geography and travel alike.
ihne-history-rome-vol-1:
Wilhelm Ihne begins his History of Rome in this first volume, from 1871, with origins, kings, and the early Republic. German rigor joins English clarity in his systematic telling. A small city on the Tiber starts its long climb toward empire in these pages.

Ihne sifts legend from record as he builds the early tale. Laws, wars, and the struggle of plebeians against patricians fill his chapters. His steady method won the work a long reign as a standard text. A generation of students learned Rome from Ihne, and the opening volume shows why: full learning, plain order, and a narrative that never loses its thread.
irving-knickerbocker-history-1809-vol-1:
Washington Irving published Knickerbocker's History of New York in 1809, pretending it was written by a Dutch antiquarian named Diedrich Knickerbocker. Irving even planted newspaper notices about the missing author as a publicity stunt. This first volume opens the mock-chronicle of Dutch New Amsterdam.

Knickerbocker begins with the creation of the world and the discovery of America, in solemn parody of real histories. He then chronicles the colony's early Dutch governors, their pipes, cabbage gardens, and quarrels with the Yankees. Irving's comedy mocks both Dutch stolidity and historical pomposity at once. The book made Irving the first American author famous abroad, and Knickerbocker became a permanent nickname for New Yorkers.
isbe-1915-vol-1:
Scottish theologian James Orr edited the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, whose first volume appeared in 1915. Orr gathered scholars to build a Bible reference that defended traditional faith with modern learning. The set aimed to answer the questions pastors and students actually asked about Scripture.

Volume 1 runs through the opening stretch of the alphabet, with articles on Bible lands, peoples, languages, and teachings. Longer pieces treat archaeology and the history behind the text, supported by maps and illustrations. The tone is conservative but the scholarship was serious for its day. The five-volume set stayed on seminary shelves for generations and is still consulted for its detailed entries on the biblical world.
jacqueline-volume-1:
Th. Bentzon, pen name of Marie Therese Blanc, opens her novel in Jacqueline, Volume 1 of the English edition. The file carries a life of Bentzon, tracing her German and Danish blood and her road into print. George Sand encouraged her, and the Revue des Deux Mondes opened its pages to her. Success came late, the essay notes, to a woman writing in France.

Jacqueline de Nailles steps forward, a Paris girl whose mother receives society. Hubert Marien has teased her since childhood as his little wife. Cousins and drawing-room rules frame her sheltered world in these chapters. Bentzon writes the girl's pride and hunger for a larger life with care. The seeds of conflict are sown quietly: a childish joke about marriage, and a man whose smile singles her out. Readers starting the volumes get author and heroine together, both women making their way inside strict French rules.
jaina-sutras-jacobi-vol-1:
Hermann Jacobi translated the first volume of the Jaina Sutras in 1884. It appeared as volume twenty-two of the Sacred Books of the East. Jainism's earliest scriptures reached English readers through Jacobi's work.

The Acaranga Sutra sets out the stern rule of Mahavira's monks. It ranks among India's oldest religious texts in any tradition. The Kalpa Sutra adds lives of the Jinas and the monks' yearly calendar. Non-violence toward all living things structures the whole way of life. Jacobi was the leading Western Jainologist of his generation. His translations present the founders' own words with scholarly care throughout.
james-bostonians-1886-vol-1:
Henry James published The Bostonians in 1886, his most political novel and a rare return to an American setting. This first volume opens the contest for the young feminist orator Verena Tarrant. James drew his Boston reformers from life, with respect and with satire in equal measure.

Olive Chancellor, a rich and intense reformer, takes the beautiful Verena under her protection after hearing her speak. Olive's cousin Basil Ransom, a reactionary young lawyer from Mississippi, arrives in Boston and decides Verena should marry instead of lecture. The battle lines form at drawing-room teas and public meetings. James builds the struggle slowly, through talk and glances, with Verena's gift as the prize.
james-portrait-of-a-lady-1881-vol-1:
Henry James published The Portrait of a Lady in 1881, the novel that made him a major figure. This first volume covers Isabel Archer's arrival in England and the great change in her fortunes. James built the book around a single vivid young woman facing her destiny with her eyes open.

Isabel, a clever American girl, is brought to England by her aunt and inherits a fortune from her uncle. The money makes her free, she believes, to live largely and choose for herself. Suitors gather: an English lord, a Boston friend, and the expatriate Gilbert Osmond, who watches from Italy. James follows Isabel's bright confidence with deepening irony. Volume One ends with her choices still open and danger gathering.
james-wings-of-the-dove-1902-vol-1:
Henry James published The Wings of the Dove in 1902, the first of the great novels of his late phase. This first volume sets the triangle in motion among London drawing rooms and an American fortune. James had brooded on the story idea, recorded in his notebooks, for a decade.

Kate Croy, poor and clever, loves the journalist Merton Densher but cannot marry him without money. Her plan takes shape when the American heiress Milly Theale arrives, rich, kind, and quietly doomed by illness. Kate maneuvers Densher toward Milly, intending that Milly's fortune will free them all. Milly, the dove of the title, senses only friendship and possibility. Volume One ends with the design laid and Venice ahead.
jataka-cowell-vol-1:
The Jataka tells the stories of the Buddha's former births, and E. B. Cowell's Cambridge edition was the first complete English version. Volume one appeared in 1895, translated from the Pali by Robert Chalmers and others under Cowell's editorship. Six volumes would follow through 1907.

In tale after tale, the future Buddha is born as a king, a merchant, a deer, a monkey, or a parrot. Each life teaches one virtue: giving, patience, courage, or truth. A verse core carries the moral, wrapped in prose story told by the Buddha himself. The tales fed Asian art and story for two thousand years, and still read as fine fables.
jefferson-writings-vol-1:
Volume One of the 1903 Lipscomb and Bergh edition of Jefferson's writings opens with his autobiography, written in 1821. Thomas Jefferson looked back at eighty on a life that shaped a nation. The early papers of his career follow.

Readers get the young lawyer and lawmaker, the drafting of the Declaration, and his work in Virginia. Letters and notes show his views on freedom, farming, and learning taking form. This edition was long treated as the standard Jefferson. For anyone meeting him in his own words, the first volume is the natural place to start. His account of drafting the Declaration has shaped how that story is told.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume-1:
Volume one of Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of John Lothrop Motley covers the historian's early life. Holmes first wrote the sketch for the Massachusetts Historical Society's Proceedings. For this book he widened it, treating controversies at length and adding many details. He calls the result an outline that may help a future biographer.

The opening chapter spans 1814 to 1827, Motley's first thirteen years. Holmes traces the family from Belfast to Falmouth, now Portland, in Maine. Thomas and Edward Motley moved to Boston in 1802 and built a lasting trade partnership. A family story from the 1708 attack on Haverhill, where a maid saved two girls, opens the line's American past.
johnson-s-lives-of-the-poets-volume-1:
Volume one of Samuel Johnson's Lives of the English Poets covers Addison, Savage, and Swift. This Cassell edition of 1888 explains in its introduction how the Lives began. Booksellers hired Johnson to write short introductions for a set of the poets. Some lives are brief, but the Life of Savage grew far beyond its plan.

Johnson wrote the Savage life at thirty-five, when he was very poor. He had known Savage in shared struggle and believed the tale the poet told. That life, the introduction argues, wins Savage a lasting place beside Addison and Swift. The later lives came when Johnson's age had about doubled. Together they remain his greatest work of criticism, mixing lives, judgment, and talk.
joshua-volume-1:
Volume one of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens the Exodus romance in its first chapters. Like the complete edition, it carries Ebers's preface to the memory of Gustav Baur. Ebers explains that the idea came to him in the desert, following the traces of the departing Hebrews. His friend Baur encouraged the plan through years of talk about the Exodus story.

Baur, a professor and counsellor worn down by illness and office, visited the greater invalid Ebers often. Those hours of lively talk, Ebers writes, count among his good ones. Death took Baur months before the book was done. So this first volume goes out under a dedication to a friend who never read it.
king-henry-iv-part-1:
King Henry IV, Part 1, by William Shakespeare, places Prince Hal beside Sir John Falstaff in lively talk. Falstaff calls them squires of the night's body and men of the moon. He jokes that their luck rises and falls like the sea. A purse snatched on Monday, he says, was spent by Tuesday morning.

The Prince answers in kind, teasing Falstaff about the hostess of the tavern. The Prince notes that Falstaff has often called her to a reckoning. Falstaff asks whether gallows will still stand when Hal becomes king. He also pleads that a thief should not hang under that reign. Their banter mixes crime, money, and kingship in one quick scene.
king-henry-vi-part-1:
King Henry VI, Part 1, by William Shakespeare, opens with a dead march and a royal funeral. Bedford, Regent of France, leads the mourning for King Henry the Fifth. Gloucester the Protector, Exeter, Warwick, Winchester, and Somerset attend him. Bedford calls on the heavens to hang with black in grief.

Bedford says England never lost a king of so much worth. Comets, Bedford says, should scourge the stars that allowed this death. Gloucester adds that England never had such a king before him. He praises the dead king's sword, arms, and fiery eyes at length. He recalls a ruler whose virtue, he says, deserved command. The grand praise leaves a hard act for the new reign.
kitto-cyclopaedia-1845-vol-1:
John Kitto published the first volume of his Cyclopaedia of Biblical Literature in 1845. Kitto's life was itself remarkable: deaf from a childhood accident and raised in poverty, he taught himself languages and traveled in the lands of the Bible. He devoted his life to making Scripture's world plain to ordinary readers.

Volume 1 opens the great Victorian Bible dictionary with entries on the lands, peoples, animals, and customs of the biblical world. Kitto insisted on explaining the text by Eastern life as it was actually lived, drawing on his own travels. Signed articles by many hands keep a high standard of care. The standard Bible reference of the English-speaking world begins here. The book sat on ministers' shelves for fifty years, and its method shaped Bible illustration ever since.
kropotkin-memoirs-revolutionist-1899-vol:
Peter Kropotkin began life as a Russian prince and ended it as an anarchist exile. Volume one of his Memoirs of a Revolutionist, from 1899, tells the first half of that arc. He recalls his childhood, his schooling in the Corps of Pages, and his service in Siberia. The wild country and its exiles awakened his science and his conscience.

His Siberian years gave him the geographic work that made his early name. They also showed him the cruelty and waste of the tsar's order. Volume one opens a two volume autobiography. Few lives cross so many worlds in one span. The telling is warm, exact, and full of people.
l-abbe-constantin-volume-1:
Ludovic Halevy wrote this French novel, first published in 1882 and crowned by the French Academy. This first volume of its English translation opens with a sketch of his life. Halevy was born in Paris in 1834, worked with Henri Meilhac on plays for almost twenty years, and turned to fiction after leaving the theatre. A preface by E. Legouvé of the French Academy follows the sketch.

The story begins at Longueval, where the old Marquise has died and her great estate must be sold and split among her grandchildren. Her friend the Abbé Constantin, the village curé, watches the home he has known for thirty years pass to strangers. Readers meet the heirs, the farms and woods on the auction bills, and the quiet priest whose kindness holds the parish together.
lameness-of-the-horse-veterinary-practit:
John Victor Lacroix wrote Lameness of the Horse as the first volume of a veterinary series. The Gutenberg edition notes that an illustrated HTML version also exists. The book speaks to working horse doctors.

Lameness was a central problem when horses powered farms and cities. A sound diagnosis could save an animal's working life. Lacroix treats causes, signs, and care in practical order. His series aimed at practitioners rather than scholars. Modern readers can see early veterinary medicine at work, before motor transport ended the horse doctor's era. Practical series like this one spread shared craft knowledge widely. Each case in it aims at a working cure.
layamon-brut-madden-vol-1:
Layamon, a priest on the Severn around the year 1200, wrote the Brut, the first chronicle of Britain in English verse. Frederic Madden's 1847 edition for the Society of Antiquaries prints the Middle English text with a literal translation. This first volume runs from Brutus of Troy to the coming of the Saxons.

Layamon retells the British kings of Geoffrey of Monmouth and Wace: the founding of Britain, the reigns of legendary kings, and the long wars with Rome. His alliterative verse keeps the beat of Old English poetry alive two centuries after the Norman conquest. Arthur looms ahead in the poem's plan. The Brut is a bridge between the old heroic world and the Arthurian age.
le-morte-d-arthur-volume-1:
Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur retells the whole King Arthur story. Volume One opens with William Caxton's preface. Book One begins with Uther Pendragon and Igraine of Cornwall.

Merlin helps Uther reach Igraine, and Arthur is conceived. Chapters follow Arthur's birth, fostering, and Uther's death. Arthur is then chosen king by a famous test. Quests, tournaments, and Round Table knights fill the books ahead. Malory gathered French and English tales into one great English prose epic. Caxton's preface defends Arthur as a worthy historical king. Malory's plain prose style carries marvels without strain.
lecky-england-18th-vol-1:
William Lecky opens his History of England in the Eighteenth Century with this first volume, from 1878. The constitution, the parties, and the manners of the age fill his broad canvas. Georgian England appears as an age of reason, commerce, and slow reform in his telling.

Lecky's learning was vast and his judgments humane throughout. He blends politics with society and ideas in one great narrative stream. Cabinets and coffee houses share his stage on equal terms. The volume began a work that Victorians ranked among their finest histories, praised for fairness, range, and a calm that never dulls into coldness.
legends-and-lyrics-part-1:
Adelaide Anne Procter wrote the poems in Legends and Lyrics, First Series. Charles Dickens supplied an introduction to her work. This text comes from the 1890 George Bell and Sons edition.

Poems include The Angel's Story, A Woman's Question, and A Doubting Heart. Others treat sorrow, homeward journeys, and cleansing fires. Procter writes in clear, song-like verse about faith and loss. Her poems were loved in Victorian homes and churches. This first series shows why she ranked among the era's most read poets. Dickens championed her work in his magazine Household Words for years. Judge Not and True Honours show her moral range. Short lyrics sit beside longer narrative legends in pleasing balance.
lesage-gil-blas-smollett-1749-vol-1:
Tobias Smollett's translation of Alain-René Lesage's Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane appeared in 1749, and Volume 1 opened the tale. Lesage, a French writer, had modeled his novel on Spanish rogue stories. Smollett, himself a novelist, gave it brisk English life.

Gil Blas, a poor young man, leaves home to make his way and falls among robbers, actors, doctors, and servants. Each master teaches him how greed and pride work in the world. The tone is comic, but the picture of society is sharp. Smollett's version naturalized the picaresque novel in English, and writers from Fielding onward learned from its loose, wandering form.
li-chi-legge-1885-vol-1:
James Legge translated the Li Chi, the Book of Rites, into English in 1885 as volumes twenty-seven and twenty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. Volume one holds the first half of the Confucian classic. The Li Chi gathers rules and essays on ritual, ceremony, mourning, music, and the order of family and state.

For Confucian China, right conduct in small acts held society together like mortar in a wall. Legge's first volume treats sacrifice, mourning dress, marriage customs, and the duties of rulers and sons. His introduction maps the text's tangled history of editing and loss. The translation, made with Chinese scholars' help, remains a standard door into ritual China. Volume two completes the work.
li-ki-legge-vol-1:
James Legge translated the first volume of the Li Ki in 1885. It appeared as volume twenty-seven of the Sacred Books of the East. The Li Ki, or Book of Rites, is Confucianism's great ritual classic.

Ceremonies for weddings, funerals, sacrifices, and court life fill the text. Moral reasoning stands behind each rule of proper conduct. The Chinese tradition treated ritual as the architecture of a civilized society. Legge, a Scottish missionary turned Oxford professor, translated all the Confucian classics. His versions dominated English study of Chinese thought for a century. Volume one opens the rites with rules for everyday courtesy and mourning.
life-and-letters-of-charles-darwin-volum:
Francis Darwin edited his father's letters for this first volume. He included an autobiographical chapter written by Charles Darwin himself. The preface says the letters aim to show Darwin's personal character. Yet Darwin's life was work, so the chapters follow his books.

Francis grouped letters by subject rather than strict chronology. His father often pursued several researches at the same time. Experiments refreshed him while large reasoning books took shape. Volume One follows the naturalist from youth toward his great theory. Several subjects often ran at once, refreshing one another, Francis explains. Resumed researches could wait years between their first trials and publication.
life-and-letters-of-lord-macaulay-volume:
George Otto Trevelyan wrote this life of his uncle, Lord Macaulay. Volume One appeared with letters woven through the biography. Trevelyan's preface to the second edition explains his method. He had spared no pains to make the first edition complete.

New letters and anecdotes still reached him after publication. Friends hunted up stray letters and recalled half-forgotten stories. He added only a sparing selection to avoid bloating the book. The result became the classic Victorian life of the great historian. Sir William Stirling Maxwell supplied one skillfully shaped reminiscence for it. Trevelyan trusted the enlarged edition's correctness in word and substance.
life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-huxley-:
Leonard Huxley edited this first volume of his father's life and letters. Thomas Henry Huxley, the great defender of evolution, is its subject. An American preface notes his special bond with transatlantic readers. His Lay Sermons had won an eager audience in the United States.

American readers prized his directness and unflinching pursuit of truth. His later lecture tour there was compared to a royal progress. Huxley used exact natural knowledge as a step toward human problems. Volume One begins the record of that wide-ranging career. Invitations to lecture in America came more than once before he accepted. His welcome there, contemporaries said, resembled a royal progress.
life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-the-qu:
Sarah Tytler wrote this life of Queen Victoria in two volumes. Lord Ronald Gower edited it and supplied an introduction. Canada registered the work by Act of Parliament in 1885. Gower's mother had enjoyed a lifelong friendship with the Queen.

His preface recalls a Wilkie chalk sketch of Victoria's hand. The study served Wilkie's picture of her first council. Gower found the sketch in a private room at Windsor Castle. Volume One thus opens with personal royal memories before the narrative. George Virtue entered the Canadian copyright for the edition. Wilkie's picture now hangs in a Windsor Castle corridor.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-1:
Part One of Twain's river book opens with the basin itself. He calls the Mississippi basin the body of the nation. Other regions are members, important through their relation to it. The basin covers about 1,250,000 square miles, he calculates.

Only the Amazon valley exceeds it in extent, Twain writes. It would contain Austria four times or France six times. British Isles or Italy would fit ten times over. European river basins shrink rudely beside these American measurements. The Lena, Amoor, and Nile reach only five-ninths its extent. Sterile Siberian basins approach it, but habitable capacity favors America.
littre-dictionary-1863-vol-1:
Émile Littré began publishing his Dictionary of the French Language in 1863, and the first volume opened the greatest French dictionary ever made. Littré was a positivist philosopher and a tireless scholar who worked on the book for decades, often through the night. His aim was scientific: to give every French word its full history.

Volume 1 carries the opening stretch of the alphabet. Each entry traces a word from its oldest forms to modern use, with quotations from the best writers as evidence. Littré treats the language's history as a branch of natural history, patient and exact. French lexicography found its crown in this work, and no later French dictionary has escaped its shadow. The first volume shows the method at full power from the very start.
lives-of-the-poets-volume-1:
Volume One of Johnson's Lives appears inside his collected Works. This seventh Works volume dates from 1825. Cowley leads the contents of the poets' lives. Denham, Milton, Butler, and Rochester follow in order.

Roscommon, Otway, Waller, and Pomfret continue the sequence. Dorset, Stepney, Philips, and Walsh bring the Restoration court in. Dryden anchors the volume as its greatest name. Smith, Duke, King, Sprat, Halifax, and Parnell close the list. Halifax closes a list drawn from the seventh Works volume. Dryden's life anchors the Restoration poets between Smith and Parnell. Sprat and Halifax close a list heavy with Restoration names.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-1:
Volume 1 opens George Meredith's novel Lord Ormont and His Aminta. The first chapters are set at a girls' school run by Mrs. Cuper. There the schoolgirl Aminta falls under the spell of Lord Ormont, a famed old soldier. Her tutor, young Matthew Weyburn, watches her with a love he cannot speak.

The volume's chapter titles promise romance and social battle ahead. Readers meet Lady Charlotte, Ormont's sister, and the world of rank and pride around him. Meredith builds the love story slowly, through talk and small turns. This opening part sets up the clash between hero worship, real love, and pride. It is the groundwork for the marriage story that follows.
lucian-works-fowler-vol-1:
H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler translated the complete works of Lucian of Samosata for Oxford in 1905. Volume one opens their four-volume English Lucian. Lucian wrote satirical dialogues in second-century Syria under Roman rule.

Gods behave badly in these pieces while philosophers are exposed as frauds. The Lover of Lies mocks believers in tall tales and sorcerers' apprentices. Alexander the False Prophet unmasks a religious con man in detail. Lucian's quick, theatrical style made him antiquity's sharpest mocker of superstition. The Fowler brothers' crisp Edwardian English suits his wit. Satirists from Erasmus to Swift learned from Lucian's methods.
luther-works-holman-vol-1:
Philadelphia's Holman edition of 1915 set out to give English readers the whole Luther, and Volume One opens the project. Early treatises and sermons from the years when a monk's protest became a revolution fill the book. The young reformer's voice arrives in English with its thunder intact.

Readers watch Luther move from academic disputes toward open break with Rome. Questions of penance, indulgences, and scripture's authority drive the pieces gathered here. The translations aim at plain readers, not only scholars. For the English-speaking world, this series became the doorway into Luther's own words. The volume captures a movement still gathering speed, before the lines hardened on every side.
lyell-principles-of-geology-vol-1:
Charles Lyell, a Scottish geologist, issued the first volume of Principles of Geology in 1830. He argued that slow forces still shaping the earth today also shaped it in the past. Rain, rivers, volcanoes, and earthquakes, given enough time, could explain ancient rocks.

Volume one lays out that method and surveys how earlier geologists had read the earth. Lyell insisted that the present is the key to the past. Charles Darwin carried the book on the Beagle voyage. Its deep view of time helped make evolution thinkable. Geologists still teach his basic approach in introductory courses today.
lyra-graeca-edmonds-loeb-vol-1:
J. M. Edmonds built Lyra Graeca to hold all that survives of the early Greek lyric poets, with his own English versions. The first Loeb volume gives Sappho of Lesbos and her fellow islander Alcaeus. Both wrote around 600 BCE, and both survive mostly in torn scraps quoted by later authors or dug from Egyptian sand.

Sappho's songs of love, prayer, and weddings include the great ode to Aphrodite, kept whole by a critic's quote. Alcaeus sings of war, wine, exile, and storms at sea that stand for storms in the state. Edmonds prints the fragments with care and fills gaps with a scholar's guesswork. These pages are the foundation of Greek lyric.
lyrical-ballads-with-other-poems-1800-vo:
Volume 1 of Lyrical Ballads, in the second edition of 1800, bears Wordsworth's name. Its famous preface explains the plan behind these poems. They take incidents of common life in the language of common men. Poems here include 'We Are Seven,' 'The Thorn,' and 'Simon Lee.'

'Lines Written Above Tintern Abbey' closes the volume in high meditation. Coleridge's 'Ancient Mariner' sails among the ballads as well. 'The Idiot Boy' and 'The Mad Mother' test the book's bold experiment. These plain tales of shepherds, children, and beggars changed English poetry. The preface became the manifesto of the Romantic age. Few volumes have ever mattered more to literature.
maccurdy-human-origins-1924-vol-1:
George Grant MacCurdy, a Yale anthropologist, published the first volume of Human Origins in 1924. He meant it as a full manual of prehistory for students. Volume one starts with the geology beneath the human story.

Chapters cover the ice ages, disputed eolith tools, and the lower Palaeolithic. MacCurdy reviews the cave and gravel finds known between the wars. New discoveries have replaced many of his dates and labels. Still, the volume shows how the field organized its evidence before radiocarbon dating existed. Teachers used it widely in American classrooms during the interwar years.
madame-chrysantheme-volume-1:
Volume 1 holds the first part of Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème. Project Gutenberg issued it as etext number 78 in its early series. The set appeared among 'The French Immortals,' crowned by the French Academy. Loti's novel takes the form of a diary he kept in Japan.

A French naval officer spends a summer at Nagasaki. There he arranges a marriage meant to last only his stay. His bride, Chrysanthème, is young, playful, and a stranger to him. The diary records houses, gardens, and his shifting feelings. This opening volume begins the season and the strange match. It sets the mood of beauty and unease that follows.
mahavastu-senart-vol-1:
Le Mahavastu, the Great Story, is a vast Sanskrit life of the Buddha told across his many lives. Émile Senart's pioneering edition opened in 1882 with this first volume. The text comes from an early school of Buddhism and grew over centuries of telling.

Volume one sets out the frame of the work and the first great runs of legend. Past lives of the Buddha, vows, and marvels crowd its Sanskrit pages. Senart printed the hard manuscript text with the care of a founder of the field. His edition first made the great story a book scholars could hold.
