maqrizi-sultans-mamlouks-quatremere-vol-:
Al-Maqrizi chronicled the Mamluk sultans of Egypt, and Quatremere's 1845 French version opens with this first volume. Slave soldiers rise to kingship in his vivid pages. Baybars and Qalawun lead the dynasty that hurled back the Mongol invasion and saved Egypt.

Cairo's courts, armies, and streets come alive in the great Arabic chronicle. Al-Maqrizi mixes annals with sharp portraits of sultans and emirs. His love for Egypt's past glows through the French dress. The work forms the chief source for the Mamluk age, an era of splendor and violence that shaped the Near East for centuries after.
marius-the-epicurean-volume-1:
Marius the Epicurean, volume one, is Walter Pater's study of a young Roman's soul. This library edition was printed at London in 1910. Its subtitle promises his sensations and ideas. Part one opens with 'The Religion of Numa' and 'White-Nights.'

Marius grows up amid the old household gods of Rome. Chapters bring a change of air, the tree of knowledge, and a golden book. 'Euphuism' and 'A Pagan End' close his boyhood's world. Part two gives him a new philosophy, a New Cyrenaicism. He journeys toward Rome, the most religious city in the world. Pater traces each fine shade of feeling in jeweled prose.
marse-henry-an-autobiography-volume-1:
Volume one of Marse Henry covers the first half of Henry Watterson's life. Watterson signed the book from Mansfield in 1919. He begins with his birth and boyhood notice of famous men.

He recalls John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and Franklin Pierce in old Washington. Then slavery breaks the Whig party and a new party rises. The volume ends as Lincoln takes office and Watterson leaves Washington for Tennessee. A run with Forrest and a bold trip through Federal lines add risk. The young Watterson learns war, print, and politics at close range.
martial-epigrams-ker-loeb-vol-1:
Martial, a Spaniard who made his name in Rome, raised the short, sharp epigram to its classic form. Walter C. A. Ker translated his poems for the Loeb series. This first volume holds books one through seven of the epigrams, more than half the full set.

Each poem is a small scene or a sting: dinner guests, legacy hunters, bad poets, doctors, and thieves pass in a few lines. Martial can flatter an emperor on one page and gut a fraud on the next. His Rome is loud, hungry, and funny. No Latin book gives the city's daily life in such quick, quotable hits.
matthew-paris-english-history-giles-vol-:
Matthew Paris, a monk of Saint Albans, wrote the Chronica Majora, the fullest English chronicle of the thirteenth century. J. A. Giles translated it, and this first volume covers the years 1235 to 1249. Matthew drew his own maps and drew the arms of the great in his margins, a chronicler who was also an artist.

Henry III rules England while Frederick II fights the pope across Europe. Mongol armies smash into Hungary and Poland, and Matthew records the terror with letters from the east. He reports parliaments, taxes, storms, and prodigies with a monk's sharp tongue. His dislike of royal waste and Roman greed runs through the years. The volume opens the grandest diary of medieval England.
melbourne-house-volume-1:
Volume one of Melbourne House came out in New York in 1865. Robert Carter and Brothers printed it at 530 Broadway. Rights were entered in 1864, the year of the first book.

The author is named only as the author of The Wide, Wide World. An old Irish tomb fronts the volume as its picture. A copy note warns that this edition was badly typeset in places. Small faults, like missing stops, were fixed, but some spellings were left as found. Chapter one starts the tale of Daisy at Melbourne House. Family talk and faith frame the child's days from the start.
memoirs-of-aaron-burr-volume-1:
Volume one of the Memoirs of Aaron Burr bears Davis's name as author. Matthew L. Davis entered the rights in 1836 in New York. The motto, I come to bury Caesar, heads the title page.

Davis says he held Burr's full trust for forty years. Burr pressed him to write once Jefferson's papers came out in print. The Ana's claims on the contest of 1801 stung Burr most. Davis found Burr proudest of his military life, more than law or politics. He offered Davis full use of all his private papers. Doubtful points, he said, he would clear up in talk.
memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-delusio:
Charles Mackay published Memoirs of Extraordinary Popular Delusions in London in 1841. Richard Bentley printed volume one in that year. A French line at the front bids readers know the follies of the mind.

The Mississippi Scheme, the South Sea Bubble, and Tulipomania lead the book. Relics, modern prophecies, and great thieves fill later chapters. One chapter treats how politics and religion shaped hair and beards. Mackay opens by saying whole nations can fix on one thing and go mad for it. Duels, ordeals, and city follies round out the first volume. Mackay writes with a storyteller's pace through hard facts.
memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherman-vol:
Volume one of Sherman's memoirs opens with his 1875 preface. William T. Sherman signed it at St. Louis on January 21. He states plainly what the book is and what it is not.

It is not a history of the war, nor a full tale of his part. It is his own memory of events, checked by his notes. He hopes it will aid the future historian of the whole war. He also hopes it will teach youth that such a country is worth a fight. Ten more years of critique fed the second edition's changes. Sherman kept his blunt tone through each round of revision.
memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-1:
Henry Hunt wrote his memoirs in His Majesty's jail at Ilchester. Volume one came out in London in 1820, from T. Dolby. A picture shows Hunt as drawn in King's Bench Prison.

The drawing was taken the morning after judgment was given on him. Lines from Pope head the book, on the faults of any work. Hunt writes of his own life as a public man and reform voice. Somerset is named on the title as the county of his jail. The jail setting gives the life a defiant, public air. Hunt tells his tale as a man judged yet unbowed.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Volume one of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens with book one. A translator's preface asks readers to judge her with more fairness. Past writers, he says, took their views from her foes at court.

Her own memoirs, now in English for the first time, may help. They were set down in a loose way, with no strict time order. The preface calls them an unplanned self portrait of a famed court lady. Her beauty and her ruthless wit stand out in that portrait. The picture list names Racine, Moliere, and Bossuet at the front. Art and church stand beside the court in her wide cast.
memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-queen-of:
Volume one of Marguerite de Valois's memoirs holds her own letters. A publisher's note says they first came out in French in 1628. That was thirteen years after her death, at age sixty three.

She was wife for many years to Henri of France, the note says. The letters tell the secret history of the French court. They span the seventeen years from 1565 to 1582. The St. Bartholomew massacre and the League's birth stand in those years. Her wit and charm won her lasting fame, the note adds. Pictures of Guise and Catherine de Medici face the letters.
memorials-and-other-papers-volume-1:
Volume one of De Quincey's Memorials and Other Papers opens with his letter. Thomas De Quincey writes to the American editor of his works. Messrs. Ticknor and Fields are the house he addresses there.

He praises them for bringing his scattered papers into one set. No legal claim bound them to share the profits, he notes. Explanatory notices lead the contents of this first volume. The Orphan Heiress, a visit to Laxton, Oxford, and Greek revolt follow. Many papers were first written under one set of hardships. Revision under fresh ones is the load he lays before readers.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-1:
Charles Merivale begins his History of the Romans under the Empire with Augustus and Tiberius, in this first volume from 1850. The republic's ashes give birth to a veiled monarchy at Rome. Power hides behind old forms while one house gathers all real rule into its hands.

Merivale writes with elegance, learning, and a quiet moral sense. He shows how liberty faded by steps few Romans noticed at first. Court whispers and frontier wars share his balanced account. The volume opened a Victorian classic of imperial Rome, a work long prized for its style, its fairness, and its somber lessons on the price of peace.
michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-swords-vol:
Volume One of Gilbert Parker's historical romance opens the story of two Huguenot refugees. Parker found their seed in a short record at the Walloon Church in Southampton. Michel de la Foret and Angele Aubert fled religious persecution in France. Their story unfolds in Elizabethan England, where Parker sets his romance.

Parker explains that the tale began as a shorter piece in Harper's Weekly. Eight years later he expanded it into the full romance called A Ladder of Swords. He wrote the first version on Jersey, in a house above Rozel Bay. This first volume carries the refugees into the dangers of the English court.
mill-principles-political-economy-1848-v:
John Stuart Mill published his Principles of Political Economy in 1848, and volume one opens the work. The book became the great Victorian synthesis of classical political economy. Mill gathers the teachings of Smith, Ricardo, and Malthus into one ordered system. Production, in his scheme, obeys laws set by nature and technique.

He treats land, labor, and capital as the agents of production. Their growth and limits fill the first volume's long inquiry. Mill writes with a clarity that made the book a university standard for decades. Volume one holds the first half of the 1848 first edition. Its calm order shaped how economics was taught.
milman-history-jews-vol-1:
Henry Hart Milman retells Jewish history as human history in this first volume, from 1829. Abraham's wanderings lead down to the founding of the Hebrew kingdom. A Christian clergyman treats the tale with reason and sympathy, not mere prophecy and miracle.

Orthodox readers were scandalized by Milman's calm, critical method at first. He asks of the Bible the same questions asked of any ancient record. Patriarchs and judges become real men in a real, harsh land. The book founded a modern way of writing Jewish history in English, and its first volume still reads as a brave act of humane scholarship.
minstrelsy-of-the-scottish-border-volume:
Walter Scott collected these historical and romantic ballads in the southern counties of Scotland. Volume One appeared in an edition dated 1806. Scott dedicated the work to the Duke of Buccleuch. The dedication honors tales that celebrated the prowess of the duke's gallant ancestors and cheered their halls.

The ballads mix true border warfare with romance and local tradition. A few pieces are modern, founded on local stories. Scott gathered the songs before print and polite manners could erase them. His collection helped create the modern interest in folk ballads, and fed his own later poetry and novels.
miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches-volu:
Volume One gathers the miscellaneous writings and speeches of Thomas Babington Macaulay. The preface explains that Macaulay always planned such a collection, reserving the copyright for it. The pieces run from his earliest to his latest work. A short biography anchors the volume: born in 1800, Trinity College, Cambridge, the bar in 1826, Parliament in 1830, India from 1834.

The volume opens with his contributions to Knight's Quarterly Magazine, written while still a young graduate. Among them is a dialogue between Milton and Cowley, which Macaulay remembered with most satisfaction. Editors invite readers to watch his famous style forming. The preface promises interest in tracing his opinions' development too.
monsieur-de-camors-volume-1: Octave Feuillet's Monsieur de Camors appears in this first volume of the English translation. The Project Gutenberg header places it thirtieth in the French Immortals series. Feuillet's novel follows a brilliant Parisian aristocrat through the society of his day. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It contains only the Gutenberg header, with title, author, and series data. Readers get the volume's identity and place in the set, but none of its scenes.
monsieur-lecoq-v-1:
Émile Gaboriau opens this detective novel on a snowy February night in Paris. It is Shrove Sunday, 186-, about eleven o'clock. A party of detectives leaves the station near the Barrière d'Italie. Their district, between the Fontainebleau road and the Seine, is the city's most dangerous quarter.

Soldiers may cross it only in parties of three or four. Homeless vagabonds and escaped criminals haunt its narrow streets after midnight. Fog hides a man's hands before his face, and slush stands ankle-deep. Into this trap walks young Lecoq, Gaboriau's detective, toward the crime that will test his method of reading clues.
motley-barneveld-vol-1:
John Lothrop Motley tells of John of Barneveld's rise in this first volume, from 1880. The Advocate of Holland builds the young Dutch Republic's greatness by law and diplomacy. Maurice of Nassau's sword defends the state that Barneveld's statecraft created and guided for thirty years.

Motley, the American historian of the Dutch revolt, opens his last great work in triumph. Treaties, councils, and foreign courts fill his rich narrative here. The founder stands at the height of his powers and fame. Few historians loved their subject's land as Motley loved Holland, and the volume shows that love in its learning, warmth, and narrative drive.
mr-crewe-s-career-volume-1:
Volume One of Winston Churchill's political novel contains its first book. The story begins with the Honourable Hilary Vane sitting for his portrait. Vane boasts he has never held office, yet trusteeships and church office crown his eminence in the state. He lives in Ripton with Euphrasia Cotton, a housekeeper with more edges than a mowing machine.

Vane's front parlour has stood unused since his wife Sarah died, thirty years before. Churchill paints a complete portrait of respectable, hidden power. Into this world comes the career of Humphrey Crewe, whose reform ambitions the later books pursue. The volume sets the old order in place before the challenge arrives.
mrs-falchion-volume-1:
Gilbert Parker began this novel in 1892, while writing his Pierre stories. He finished it in the summer of 1893. It first came out in three volumes, the custom of the day. Parker tells all this in a frank introduction.

He chose not to print it in parts in a magazine. He wanted readers to take the whole tale at one gasp. The publisher's reader doubted, but Mr. Methuen backed the book. Reviews called Parker a coming novelist and praised the character work. This first volume holds that introduction and the opening half of his first novel's story.
muqaddimah-prolegomenes-slane-1863-tome-:
Baron William MacGuckin de Slane translated Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah into French in three volumes, from 1863 to 1868. Tome one, published in 1863, opens the Prolegomena, the great introduction Ibn Khaldun wrote in 1377 for his universal history. The text here is de Slane's French, the standard scholarly edition of its age.

Ibn Khaldun asks how societies rise, bind together, and decay, and answers with his theory of group feeling. Geography, climate, and the contrast of desert and city frame his inquiry. De Slane, an Irish-born scholar in French service, worked from fine manuscripts for the Notices et extraits series. His version carried Ibn Khaldun to European historians. Tome one lays the theory's foundations.
my-life-volume-1:
Richard Wagner dictated this life story to his wife over many years. She had wished him to tell it for family and close friends. A few copies were printed at their own cost to guard the tale. Wagner insists its worth lies in plain, unadorned truth.

Names and dates are given exactly, he warns in the preface. For that reason the book could not be published until after his death. Volume one runs from 1813 to 1850, ending at Dresden. It covers his childhood, schooling, and first posts. The authorized translation lets English readers hear the composer judge his own rise in his own words.
nara-m887-doctors-trial-roll-1:
Roll One of archive series M887 holds transcripts of the Nuremberg Doctors Trial. After World War Two, American judges tried Nazi doctors for crimes on prisoners. The United States National Archives keeps the full record.

Witnesses describe medical tests done without consent in the camps. Prosecutors lay out charges of murder and torture in cold detail. Doctors defend their acts with claims of orders and science. The reading is grim but vital. These pages form a base record for medical ethics law, built from the words spoken in court. No reader comes away from it unmoved.
narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers-volum:
Thomas De Quincey's first volume here holds three long tales. The Household Wreck leads, then The Spanish Nun. Flight of a Tartar Tribe closes the volume. Each tale turns on peril, flight, or a home in ruins.

The Household Wreck begins with praise and blame of weakness. All weakness is suffering and shame, De Quincey declares. Man cannot hold his crown of flowers for an hour, he writes. Life's pomps rest on hollow ground, he warns at length. His dense, musical sentences swell like organ music. The tales show the opium essayist as a bold, strange storyteller of doom and rescue.
nasa-tm-19630004890-free-flight-tests-to:
Joseph H. Judd and Gerard E. Woodbury of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-437. It reports free-flight tests of slim triangular pyramid shapes. These shapes were candidates for gliding back from space. Models flew at speeds up to Mach 1.5, half again sound's speed.

Free-flight tests launch real models, not tunnel mounts, for true motion. The pyramid forms were slender, with flat faces and sharp edges. Judd and Woodbury watched how the models flew and held their path. Catalog notes put the speed range from Mach 0.6 to 1.5. The work helped judge whether sharp pyramid craft could return safely and land under control.
nasa-tm-19650012942-saturn-monthly-progr:
Marshall Space Flight Center issued this Saturn monthly progress report for January 16 to February 16, 1964. It covers the Saturn I, Saturn IB, and Saturn V rocket programs. On January 29, SA-5 became the first Saturn to carry a live second stage, and it launched from Cape Kennedy after a failed attempt two days earlier.

Other entries track checkout work at Marshall and stage work in Santa Monica. An asterisk marks items carried over from the last report. Monthly reports like this one kept a huge program visible to its managers. They also preserve, in plain sequence, how the Saturn rockets moved toward flight.
nasa-tm-19650023622-satellite-situation-: Volume 5, number 15 of the satellite situation report is preserved here only as garbled scan characters. No readable satellite list, table, or date can be recovered from the hosted sample of this NASA Space Operations Control Center report. The title and catalog note alone identify its subject as the current situation of orbiting satellites.
nasa-tm-19660026686-research-achievement:
Research Achievements Review, Series No. 10, is a 1965 volume from the Research and Development Operations office at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Rather than a single study, the issue collects short reports on recent progress across the center's quality and checkout work for space vehicles.

One section sets out a guideline document for analyzing and checking out space vehicle stages before flight. Other sections describe gains in automated checkout, including a digital event evaluator and a computer method for calibrating instruments. Further pieces cover checkout display needs, control methods used during testing, and single parameter testing. The catalog record also lists work on testing structures without damaging them and on testing electronic parts.
nasa-tm-19710010494-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Volume 2 of Panel 1's report traces the manufacturing and test history of Apollo 13's oxygen tank number two. Panel 1 ran the spacecraft incident investigation for the Manned Spacecraft Center after the April 1970 explosion. This volume follows the tank's life on its cryogenic shelf, as installed in Spacecraft 109.

Sections cover the tank's time at Kennedy Space Center, its fan motor performance, quantity gaging checks, and system purity. A long part examines the detanking incident, when the tank could not be emptied normally before flight. It reviews ground equipment, spacecraft checks, the special detanking procedure, management actions, and the launch rationale. Supporting data lists the discrepancy reports, waivers, and sampling results behind the account.
nex-pelle-the-conqueror-vol-1:
Martin Andersen Nexo begins his vast Danish epic in the first English volume of Pelle the Conqueror, the part called Boyhood. Young Pelle lands in Denmark with his father, Lasse. Both hire out as farm servants, and the boy sees hard masters and low pay up close.

Through Pelle's eyes, readers feel the hunger, cold, and small joys of poor farm life. Lasse dreams of a better lot while bowing to those above him. The boy begins to sense that the order of things is unjust. Nexo builds the base of a famed novel of working-class life with warmth and detail.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-1:
Philip Schaff's Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, opens in 1886 with Augustine: his Confessions and Letters, plus a sketch of his life and work. The set became the standard English patristic library. No better door into Augustine exists in the series.

The Confessions tell Augustine's story: his wild youth, his years among the Manichaeans, and his conversion in a Milan garden. The last books turn from story to thought, on memory, time, and the opening of Genesis. A selection of his letters follows, showing the bishop at work. Few books in any age bare a soul so fully.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-1:
The second series of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, edited by Philip Schaff and Henry Wace from 1890, opens with Eusebius of Caesarea. The volume holds his Church History, his Life of Constantine, and his Oration in Praise of Constantine. Eusebius wrote in the early fourth century, as persecution gave way to empire.

The Church History is the first of its kind: bishops, martyrs, heresies, and writers from the apostles to Constantine, built from documents he quotes at length. Without it, most early church history would be guesswork. The Life then turns courtly, praising the first Christian emperor in high style. The volume is the foundation stone of church history writing.
niebuhr-history-rome-vol-1:
Barthold Georg Niebuhr published his History of Rome to challenge the old stories told about the city's first centuries. The first English edition, translated by Julius Charles Hare and Connop Thirlwall, appeared in 1828. Volume one takes Rome from its legendary founding through the early republic.

Niebuhr treated Rome's cherished legends the way a lawyer tests a witness. He compared sources, spotted later inventions, and rebuilt the story of early Roman land, law, and class conflict from firmer ground. Many of his guesses were bold, and later scholars corrected plenty. Still, his demand for proof over tradition made him a founder of modern source criticism in history.
night-and-morning-volume-1:
Volume one of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning holds the start of his novel. A note in this copy points readers to a corrected five volume set elsewhere in Project Gutenberg. The title page in the sample names the works of Edward Bulwer Lytton, Lord Lytton. Book one is the part given here.

Lytton's own words in the sample turn on schooling and effort. Cheap books and popular treatises, he warns, cannot give knowledge without labour. Toil divorced from knowledge robs knowledge of its best gift, the strength that exercise brings. Life, he says, is the great school, not books alone. The novel's first book grows from that stern creed.
no-defense-volume-1:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's No Defense, in this copy, oddly lists the contents of all three books. The tale itself starts with Book one. Two men meet, a messenger comes, and a quarrel leads to a duel. Erris Boyne is killed, and Dyck goes to prison.

Dyck's father visits him there, and a letter arrives from Sheila. The first chapter opens with a cheery warning to Dyck about meeting at the sessions or the assizes. Parker's narrator calls that the humour and incongruity of Irish life. The listed later books promise the West Indies, a mutiny, and Salem. This volume gives the crime and the fall.
normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its-anci:
Part one of Gordon Home's Normandy presents the opening portion of his book on the scenery and romance of its ancient towns. Home dated the work at Epsom in October 1905. This part carries the same contents list as the whole, with coloured and line illustrations named up front. Chapter one treats some features of Normandy.

The banks of the Seine and Rouen, ancient capital of Normandy, come early. Evreux and the road to Bernay follow, then Lisieux and the romantic town of Falaise. From Argentan the road runs to Avranches and Mont St Michel. Home draws the towns he describes, so word and picture travel together for the reader.
north-america-volume-1:
Anthony Trollope travelled through the United States from August 1861 to May 1862, and North America tells that trip. Chapman and Hall first published it in two volumes in 1862. An editor's note says he visited every state that did not secede, except California. Volume one opens with Newport, Rhode Island.

Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont come next, then Lower and Upper Canada. A chapter weighs the Canadas' tie to Great Britain, and Niagara gets one of its own. The road runs north and west, down to the Mississippi and up its upper course. Trollope adds chapters on New York, its state constitution, Boston, and Lowell. The war then raging frames the whole.
northern-lights-volume-1:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights holds the first four tales of his western set. A Lodge in the Wilderness opens the volume. Once at Red Man's River and The Stroke of the Hour follow. Buckmaster's Boy closes this first group. The whole contents of five volumes are listed up front.

Parker's introduction, printed here, sets the tales a generation after Pierre and His People. Pierre and Shon McGann lived, he says, in a lone and pathetic world. The railway ended those conditions for good. Towns rose, settlers poured in, and the old isolation faded. Parker wrote to catch the fleeting marks of that older Far West before they vanished.
old-mortality-volume-1:
Sir Walter Scott wrote the Covenanter novel Old Mortality. Volume one is the first half of that work. The editor's introduction traces the book to May 1816. Joseph Train brought Scott stories from Galloway that spring. A schoolmaster's joke helped create the narrator figure.

Henry Morton enters a land torn by religious war. Old Mortality tends the graves of fallen martyrs. His wanderings give the novel its haunting frame. Scott blends real history with invented lives and loves. Readers meet both zeal and mercy in this volume. Train also brought a Rob Roy relic in his hand. Scott's den held a famed portrait of Claverhouse, Train found.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-1:
George Meredith published this novel in the year 1897. Volume one holds the first part of the work. It opens across London Bridge with Victor Radnor. Nataly, his partner, enters in chapter six. Skepsey, their devoted servant, moves in chapter ten.

The couple glimpse their coming scourge by chapter eleven. Book two treats dumbness within a loving household. A drive to Paris and a patriot abroad follow. Nesta's imaginings and her suitors fill later chapters here. Meredith packs the prose with wit, irony, and psychology. Readers should continue with the later volumes for the end. This volume sets ambition and secret shame in motion.
orderic-vitalis-ecclesiastical-history-f:
Orderic Vitalis, born in England of a Norman father and raised in a monastery in Normandy, spent his life writing the Ecclesiastical History. Thomas Forester translated the work, and this first volume appeared in 1853. Orderic's thirteen books form the fullest Norman chronicle of the twelfth century.

He begins with the life of Christ and the early church, then turns to Normandy, its dukes, and its monasteries. His own house of Saint Evroul gets a loving, detailed tale. Orderic writes as a monk between two peoples, English by birth and Norman by training. His sympathy runs to the small and the beaten. The set that opens here is a treasury of the age.
oscar-wilde-his-life-and-confessions-vol: Volume one of Frank Harris's Oscar Wilde, His Life and Confessions is a biography of the Irish playwright and wit. Harris knew him personally. The hosted sample of this edition, however, contains no page of the biography itself. It consists entirely of the Project Gutenberg header and license text. That header gives the title, the author, and a January 2003 release date. It also notes this is volume one of two. So this note reports only what the front matter establishes. It describes none of the life the volume covers.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-1:
E. W. West opened his Pahlavi Texts series in 1880 with volume five of the Sacred Books. The volume translates three Zoroastrian works from Middle Persian. West devoted his career to rescuing Iran's post-conquest religious literature.

The Bundahishn, meaning Creation, tells how the world was made and ordered. It serves as Persia's Genesis, with cosmology and a final renovation. The Bahman Yasht prophesies the end times and coming saviors. The Shayast la-Shayast sets out ritual law, what is fit and unfit. Together they give myths of ancient Iran rescued from Middle Persian. West's five volumes remain a foundation of Zoroastrian studies.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-1:
John Gorham Palfrey begins his History of New England with the Pilgrims' landing, in this first volume from 1858. Puritans found Massachusetts and build a godly commonwealth in the wilderness. Sermons, charters, and town meetings shape a new society on a stern and hopeful plan.

Palfrey, a Unitarian minister and scholar, writes the classic nineteenth-century account. He honors the founders' faith while tracing their laws and wars. The wilderness gives nothing freely in his sober, detailed telling. His work defined how New England remembered its own origins for generations, and it remains the standard doorway into the Puritan experiment in America.
pappus-collection-hultsch-vol-1:
Pappus of Alexandria, writing around 320 CE, gathered the best of Greek geometry into his Mathematical Collection. Friedrich Hultsch edited the Greek text with a Latin version in 1876. This first volume holds books two through five of the Collection. No English version in the public domain exists.

Pappus sums up lost works by Euclid, Apollonius, and others, and adds proofs and tools of his own. His name lives in the centroid theorem that geometry books still teach. Because so much Greek math is lost, Pappus is often the only witness to what the great geometers proved. The volume opens the richest single source for the lost world of Greek geometry.
pareto-cours-economie-politique-1896-fr-:
Vilfredo Pareto lectured at Lausanne in 1896 and 1897, and tome one of his Cours d'economie politique appeared in 1896. The lectures founded the Lausanne school of economics. General equilibrium, the balance of all markets at once, forms their core. The volume also gives a first statement of what became Pareto optimality.

A state is optimal, in that idea, when no one can gain without another's loss. Pareto builds the theory in French, with heavy use of math. No public domain English translation exists, so the French original stands. Tome one opens a two volume course. Economists rank it among the field's founding texts.
pareto-systemes-socialistes-1902-fr-vol-:
Pareto surveyed socialist systems at Lausanne in lectures printed as Les Systemes socialistes in 1902. Tome one begins the survey in French. He moves from the early utopian planners toward the schools of his own day. Marx receives long and serious treatment among the later systems.

Pareto tests each scheme against facts about human nature and elites. His tone stays cool, more surgeon than preacher, throughout. The lectures show the economist of Lausanne turning his tools on socialism. No public domain English translation exists for the work. Tome one opens a two volume set. It pairs with his later sociology in revealing key. His judgments remain sharp and quotable.
pareto-trattato-sociologia-generale-1916:
Pareto's masterwork of sociology, the Trattato di sociologia generale, began with volume one in 1916. The Italian text presents his theory of residues and derivations. Residues are the deep, steady drives under human conduct. Derivations are the shifting reasons people give to dress those drives up.

Elites rise and fall in a slow circulation that his theory tracks. Pareto treats much of politics and belief as surface over these depths. The work made him a founder of modern sociology, admired and disputed. No public domain English translation exists. Volume one opens a two volume set. Its cold eye on human motives still unsettles.
parkman-half-century-conflict-vol-1:
Parkman's Half-Century of Conflict opens the wars of the 1700s in America. Volume 1, from 1892, forms part of his France and England series. Queen Anne's War starts the long fight for the continent here.

Raids, sieges, and sea fights fill Parkman's fast, vivid narrative pages. He writes with the smell of pine smoke and gunpowder in the air. French and English settlers pay the price of empire in blood. Native nations weigh each side and strike for their own ends. Wilderness war has seldom had a better teller than Parkman at his best. His research in French archives backs every vivid scene he paints.
passages-from-the-american-notebooks-vol:
Volume 1 of Passages from the American Notebooks prints selections from Nathaniel Hawthorne's private journals. The entries begin in Salem in June 1835, when Hawthorne was a young, still obscure writer. He records walks along the shore in close detail, noting sea-weed, driftage, fishes, and stones.

Other entries watch pigs at the almshouse or sunlight falling on a jail wall. The value of the notebooks lies in this patient attention. Readers can see the raw material of Hawthorne's fiction here, small scenes he observed years before they fed his tales and romances.
passages-from-the-english-notebooks-volu:
Volume 1 of Passages from the English Notebooks presents the first part of the journals Hawthorne kept while living in England. An editor's preface explains why the private notebooks were printed at all. Hawthorne had asked that no biography of him be attempted, and his family judged his own journals the truest sketch of his life.

The editor kept the manuscripts' order and wording, omitting only a few passages. What remains is a daily record of English places, people, and customs, written by a quiet American observer. It shows the working mind behind the famous romances.
passages-from-the-french-and-italian-not:
Volume 1 of Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks covers the first stretch of Hawthorne's continental travels. It begins in January 1858, when the family left a bitterly cold London before daylight. They travelled by train to Folkestone, crossed the Channel to Boulogne, and went on to Paris.

The entries linger on the journey itself, the waiting rooms, market carts, and icy windows. Hawthorne observes France as a newcomer fresh from years in England. This volume sets the scene for the Italian travels that follow, and shows his notebook style at its most observant.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Pausanias toured Greece in the second century CE and described everything he saw. J. G. Frazer translated the Description of Greece in 1898, and volume one opens the work. Pausanias begins in Attica, the territory of Athens.

Temples, statues, tombs, and local legends crowd his itinerary. He records myths at the very shrines where Greeks told them. Frazer's commentary, in later volumes, tests every statement against archaeology. The ancient guidebook remains indispensable for classical Greece today. Whole sanctuaries can be reconstructed from Pausanias's careful notes alone. Volume one gives the traveler's text that the commentary volumes then unpack.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 1 of volume 1 of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs carries his preface, dated August 1888. He dedicates the record to his comrades of the War of the Rebellion and to his children, and offers it as information for the future historian. He warns that he makes no pretension to literary merit.

Chapter one covers ancestry, birth, and early education. His parents emigrated from County Cavan, Ireland, in 1830, selling a leasehold to fund the crossing. Young Sheridan clerked in a grocery store, won an appointment to West Point, was suspended over a fistfight, clerked again, and graduated.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-1:
Part 1 of Grant's Personal Memoirs begins with his famous preface. Ruined by a business partner's fraud and living on borrowed money, Grant took up his pen for the Century Magazine because he needed the income. He promises to avoid injustice to anyone, National or Confederate, and warns of errors of omission in so large a subject.

Grant explains that much of the work was written before he knew his health was critical, and later finished in weakness, with his sons verifying facts from the records. The opening part carries his ancestry, youth, West Point, and the start of his soldier's life.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-volume-1:
Volume 1 of Grant's Personal Memoirs carries the same preface that opens the part editions. Grant tells how a fall, a partner's rascality, and borrowed money pushed a reluctant man into authorship. He wrote the first volume before he supposed his health critical, then worked on almost to the point of death.

His sons helped verify every statement of fact from the records, while the comments remain his own. The volume itself runs from Grant's Ohio boyhood through West Point and the Mexican War to the western campaigns of the Civil War, ending around Vicksburg. Its clarity made it an American classic.
personal-recollections-of-joan-of-arc-vo: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of volume 1 of Mark Twain's Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, a quotation and the contents, with no narrative text visible. The quotation, from Louis Kossuth, claims Joan is the only person of either sex to hold supreme command of a nation's armies at seventeen. The contents open in Domremy, with wolves in Paris, the fairy tree, and Joan's voices, then move into court and camp.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Volume 1 of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People opens his five-volume set of far north tales. In his general introduction Parker explains that a 1912 subscription edition carried a special introduction for each volume, setting out how each work fit the scheme of his literary life.

Three long tales fill this first volume: The Patrol of the Cypress Hills, God's Garrison, and A Hazard of the North. Their titles point to the set's world of Mounted Police patrols, lonely posts, and danger on the frontier. Parker notes that most of his stories came from incidents or characters he had known or heard of intimately, which gives the fiction a reported, lived-in feel.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-1:
Plato's dialogues, in Benjamin Jowett's classic 1892 English translation, fill five volumes; this first volume holds nine works. Charmides, Lysis, and Laches ask what temperance, friendship, and courage are. Protagoras stages a great debate on whether virtue can be taught.

Euthydemus mocks two trick arguers, while Cratylus turns to the nature of names and language. Phaedrus, on love and rhetoric, is among Plato's most beautiful works. The volume closes with the Symposium, the drinking party where Socrates and his friends each praise love in turn. Jowett's smooth prose made these the standard English Plato for generations.
plautus-comedies-riley-1852-vol-1:
Henry Thomas Riley translated the comedies of Plautus into plain English prose for Bohn's library in 1852. Volume one holds ten plays, from Trinummus and Miles Gloriosus to the Menaechmi and Aulularia. Plautus, Rome's earliest great comic writer, filled his stage with trickster slaves, braggart soldiers, and mixed-up twins.

The Menaechmi, a comedy of twin confusion, later fed Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors. Aulularia's miser guarding his pot of gold became a stock figure for Europe. Riley chose prose so English readers could follow every twist of the plots. With volume two, his set completes the surviving Plautus. The library's older two-play selection is superseded by this full text.
poems-in-two-volumes-volume-1:
William Wordsworth, already known as the author of Lyrical Ballads, published his Poems in Two Volumes. This first volume gathers many of the short lyrics on which his fame rests. A Latin motto promises that his muse will speak in a graver tone later, when time brings safer fruits. The contents mix sonnets, songs, and tales of ordinary people, all in the plain style Wordsworth defended as poetry's true language.

Pieces here include To the Daisy, She Was a Phantom of Delight, the Character of the Happy Warrior, and I Travelled Among Unknown Men. Others tell of the sailor's mother, the affliction of Margaret, and the seven sisters of Binnorie. Read together, they show Wordsworth's great subject clearly: strong feeling recalled from small moments, a flower. A bird, a child, a grave, until the small moment opens into a philosophy of life.
poems-volume-1:
George Meredith's Poems appear in the Surrey Edition issued by the Times Book Club in London in 1912. Three years after his death, with a picture of his cottage at Box Hill on the cover. Meredith was better known as a novelist, yet he and many later readers thought the poems his finest work, dense, musical meditations on nature and the mind. This first volume of three gathers his earlier and shorter verse.

Contents open with Chillianwallah, his ringing poem on the Sikh war battle, then the Doe fragment, Beauty Rohtraut. The Olive Branch, and love songs and nature pieces such as the Wild Rose and the Snowdrop. Meredith's sonnets and lyrics demand slow reading; every line thinks. The Surrey Edition, named for his beloved county, presented the poet whole to a public that had largely caught up with him only at the end.
polybius-histories-shuckburgh-vol-1:
Polybius, a Greek statesman held hostage in Rome, wrote his Histories to explain Rome's rise. Evelyn Shuckburgh translated the work, and volume one covers Books 1 through 9. The Punic Wars and Rome's constitution stand at its center.

Polybius asks how Rome conquered the Mediterranean world within fifty-three years. He explains Rome's mixed constitution of consuls, senate, and people with admiration. The First and Second Punic Wars unfold with a participant's respect for facts. Polybius had served as a cavalry officer and diplomat himself. Fair-minded and analytical, he remains a historian's historian. Shuckburgh's English stays lucid throughout.
poor-jack-1:
Captain Marryat's Poor Jack stands here in the tenth volume of his works with illustrations, arranged as a long run of fifty-one numbered chapters and a finale. The front matter maps the whole enterprise before the story starts: a frontispiece portrait of Jack, Fisher's Alley where he grows up. Anderson reading the Bible to the boy, and Anderson again bringing news of the battle of the Nile, the victory that shapes the family's fate.

The chapter count itself tells readers what kind of book this is: a full-dress naval novel of a poor boy's rise. Built episode by episode like a sailor's yarn that keeps finding one more adventure. Marryat wrote from service experience, and the illustrated edition dresses his tale for the family shelf. This presentation emphasizes the cycle of pictures, and Poor Jack became a standard gift book for boys.
prince-zilah-volume-1:
Jules Claretie's Prince Zilah opens in this first volume. Issued as number fourteen in the series of French Immortals crowned by the French Academy and the first of Claretie's works in that series. The volume carries the novel's first half: the Hungarian prince Andras Zilah, an exile in Paris after his country's failed struggles. Moves through the salons of the capital, and his love for the beautiful Marsa begins under the shadow of her secret.

Claretie, journalist, academician, and director of the Comédie-Française, filled his fiction with the Paris he reported daily, its theaters, newspapers, and fashionable marriages. A split-volume issue like this one, sold to the circulating-library trade, let English readers take the romance in two sittings. The first volume ends, as serial logic demands, with the prince's happiness built and the blackmail that will test it already loaded offstage.
proclus-commentary-timaeus-taylor-vol-1:
Proclus, a pagan philosopher of late Athens, wrote long notes on Plato's Timaeus. Thomas Taylor translated them into English in 1820. Volume One opens his reading of Plato's tale of creation.

Proclus treats the Timaeus as sacred truth about gods and cosmos. He unfolds its myths into a full system of ranks and causes. Taylor, himself a devoted Platonist, keeps the tone lofty. The work is hard but rich for patient minds. It shows how the last pagans read their master: as a theologian, not just a thinker. Taylor's notes add help for modern readers.
queen-victoria-1: Queen Victoria, by Lytton Strachey, is shown here in the New York edition of Harcourt, Brace and Company, 1921, by its title page and contents alone. The ten chapters run in a set order. They are Antecedents, Childhood, Lord Melbourne, and Marriage. Lord Palmerston and Last Years of Prince Consort follow. Widowhood, Gladstone and Lord Beaconsfield, Old Age, and The End complete the list. A bibliography and list of references in the notes follow.
quintilian-institutio-butler-loeb-vol-1:
Quintilian taught rhetoric in Rome and ran the empire's most famed school of speaking. His Institutio Oratoria sets out the whole training of an orator, from the cradle to the court. H. E. Butler translated it for the Loeb series, and this first volume holds books one and two.

The work opens with the choice of a nurse, the first lessons of a child, and the right way to run a school. Quintilian weighs play against the rod and Greek against Latin. Book two moves to the rhetoric master and the first drills in speech. It is the fullest plan of education that the ancient world left us.
ragged-lady-volume-1:
Ragged Lady, volume one, by William Dean Howells, begins with Mr. and Mrs. Lander arguing in a carry-all at a fork in the road during their first summer at Middlemount. She recites the troubles his refusal to ask directions has caused before; the horse, meanwhile, crops sweet fern and blueberry bushes impartially on either side of the wheel-track.

She threatens to get out and ask herself. The dry little man snaps the reins at that. He nearly oversets the carriage. Then he drives her to the door of an unfinished house. The drive serves as a sort of apology. The place has been lived in a year, yet its window casings are merely set in place and its trim waits on some future impulse of the builder.
ranke-history-england-vol-1:
Leopold von Ranke reshaped how history is written in the modern age. His History of England reached English in John Oxenford's 1875 translation. Volume 1 treats the sixteenth century, from Henry VII to the roots of reform.

Ranke works from state papers and the reports of envoys abroad. He weighs kings, courts, and councils with cool, even judgment throughout. The Tudor rise and the first cracks in the old church fill his pages. His famed aim was to show the past as it truly was. Readers meet that method here at full strength, on England's turning age.
ranke-reformation-germany-vol-1:
Sarah Austin's 1845 translation opens Ranke's History of the Reformation in Germany. Volume 1 begins with Luther's rise and the revolt against Rome. The indulgence quarrel and the Diet of Worms anchor the early tale.

Ranke commands the archives like no writer before him in this field. He traces deep causes in church wealth, German pride, and print. Luther stands forth as monk, rebel, and voice of a nation. Princes hedge, peasants stir, and the old order cracks year by year. The religious revolution of the age finds its sure guide here. Few opening volumes carry such weight of proof and story together.
repertory-of-the-comedie-humaine-part-1: A publisher's header alone opens Part I of the Repertory of the Comedie Humaine, and it gives the part's span in its title line: A through K. The header places the item in a series of works by or about Honoré de Balzac. No preface, no title page, and no entry from the alphabetical list itself follows in the pages at hand. A reader can note the work's name, its first part's letter range, and its Balzac series place, but the entries for those letters are not shown here.
reymont-the-peasants-vol-1:
Autumn opens Reymont's vast epic The Peasants, and this first English volume sets the village year in motion. The Boryna family works its land as days shorten and frost nears. Old Maciej rules his farm and sons with a hard, proud hand.

Marriage plans, land hunger, and local feuds stir beneath the harvest calm. Reymont ties each drama to the turning of the seasons and soil. His peasants speak, quarrel, and feast in scenes of great earthy force. The four-volume work later won him the Nobel Prize, and this opening shows the full method: a village as a whole world.
rhoda-fleming-volume-1: A publisher's header, in the plain style of early free e-texts, is the only front matter for volume one of Rhoda Fleming by George Meredith. The header gives the title, the author's name, and English as the language. It places the item in a series of works by George Meredith, as the twenty-seventh of that series. No contents page, preface, or opening chapter of the novel follows it in the pages at hand. What portion of Rhoda's story this first volume holds cannot be told from these pages.
roger-hoveden-annals-riley-vol-1:
Roger of Hoveden, a clerk in the household of Henry II, wrote a chronicle that runs on from Bede to his own times. Henry Riley translated it, and this first volume, from 1853, ends in the year 1192. Roger had access to royal letters and records, and he copies many of them into his tale.

The reign of Henry II fills the volume: the Becket quarrel and murder, wars in France, and the young kings' revolts. Roger writes plain annals, year by year, with charters and letters set in full. That dry habit makes him gold for scholars of the Angevin state. His chronicle is one of the key sources for the rule of Henry II.
roger-wendover-flowers-history-giles-vol:
Roger of Wendover, a monk of Saint Albans, wrote the Flores Historiarum, the Flowers of History, from the creation of the world down to his own day. J. A. Giles translated the work, and this first volume appeared in 1849. Roger died in 1236, and Matthew Paris took his chronicle up and made it greater.

The early books sweep through biblical and Roman times toward the kings of England. Roger gathers what the older chronicles said and arranges it year by year. His own voice grows stronger as the tale nears his lifetime. The Saint Albans line of chroniclers, the best in medieval England, starts in these pages. Giles's version opens that tradition to English readers.
romance-three-kingdoms-brewitt-taylor-19:
C. H. Brewitt-Taylor translated Luo Guanzhong's Romance of the Three Kingdoms into English in 1925. Volume one holds chapters one through sixty of China's great historical novel. As the Han dynasty falls in the second century, warlords carve China into three rival kingdoms: Wei, Shu, and Wu.

Liu Bei and his sworn brothers, the strategist Zhuge Liang, and the mighty Cao Cao drive the early wars. Brewitt-Taylor, a customs officer long resident in China, made the first complete English version. The novel mixes chronicle history with legend, duels, and stratagems on a vast scale. Chinese readers have ranked it among their four great classical novels for centuries. Volume two completes the story.
roughing-it-part-1:
Part 1 of Roughing It, by Mark Twain, carries an 1880 title page and a warm gift inscription to Calvin H. Higbie of California. Twain calls Higbie an honest man, a genial comrade, and a steadfast friend. The book is inscribed in memory of the curious time when the two were millionaires for ten days. In the preface Twain calls the work a personal narrative and a record of several years of varied wandering in the Far West.

Twain says the book aims to help a resting reader pass an idle hour, not to press him with deep thought or science. Still, facts stew out of him, and those facts concern the silver-mining fever in Nevada. He saw its rise, growth, and peak in person, on the ground. No books, he notes, had been written on that episode by men who were there.
rule-a-wife-and-have-a-wife-beaumont-fle:
Rule a Wife and Have a Wife opens Act One, Scene One of the Beaumont and Fletcher works as edited by A. R. Walker, with Juan de Castro and Michael Perez on stage talking of war. Perez asks whether Castro's companies are full. Castro answers no, and not for a month yet, by his reckoning. Perez replies that his own command still picks up men as money holds out. Young gallants, both agree, are going to the wars in numbers, green and keen in equal measure.

Castro warns that war looks like a fine dream to young, hot spirits, and that time and hard knocks will cool those visions. He then turns to a new recruit, Don Leon, put forward by noble friends for a post under him. Leon is a fine, tall fellow with a giant's promise in his looks, Castro says, and he has served before.
sacred-books-east-vol-13-vinaya-texts-1:
Volume thirteen of the Sacred Books of the East opens the Vinaya Texts, the rule books of Buddhist monks, in translations by T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg from 1881. The Vinaya is the discipline basket of the Pali canon. Part one holds the Patimokkha and the start of the Mahavagga.

The Patimokkha lists the 227 rules monks recite together each fortnight, from grave offenses down to points of manners. The Mahavagga then tells how the Buddha founded the order, set the ordination rite, and framed the rains retreat. Every rule comes with the story that caused it. The volume shows Buddhism organizing itself to last.
sacred-laws-aryas-buhler-vol-1:
Georg Buhler translated the first volume of the Sacred Laws of the Aryas in 1879. It appeared as volume two of the Sacred Books of the East. The volume holds the Dharma Sutras of Apastamba and Gautama.

These terse codes govern duty, diet, marriage, penance, and life's stages. They are older than the famous Laws of Manu. Students, householders, and hermits each receive their proper rules. Buhler was a leading Sanskritist who had worked in India itself. His translations showed Hindu law in its earliest written form. The sutras' compressed style assumes teachers explaining them aloud. Buhler's notes supply much of that missing explanation for readers.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-1:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, issued Samantha Among the Brethren in parts, and the portion shown here is headed Part 1, with pictures, dated 1890. The dedication gives the book to all women who work, trying to bring into dark lives the brightness and hope of a better country. The preface opens in Samantha's sitting room. Her companion Josiah Allen watches her take her inkstand off the mantelpiece. She carries it with a calm and majestic gait to the corner of the table set aside for her writing, and he asks what she is going to tackle now.

Samantha answers with quite a good deal of dignity that she will tackle the cause of eternal justice. Josiah asks if there is anything else, looking sort of uneasy at her. She notes, in an aside, that the man realizes his shortcomings a good deal of the time.
sandra-belloni-volume-1: Volume 1 of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni is identified only in Project Gutenberg header matter, with no title page or chapter text in the portion shown here. The header gives the title, names Meredith as author, and lists a release date of September 2003. The file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4413, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. Pat Castevans and David Widger are named as the people who produced the electronic text.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-1:
Julius Eggeling translated the Satapatha Brahmana for the Sacred Books of the East series in 1882. Volume one opens his five-volume rendering of the great Sanskrit ritual text. The Satapatha is the most important of the Brahmanas.

Brahmana prose explains the meaning behind every Vedic sacrifice, rite by rite. Eggeling's first volume covers the opening books on major offerings. Myths appear inside the ritual instructions, preserving India's oldest stories. Priests used the Satapatha as a working manual for grand ceremonies. Eggeling's Victorian scholarship made the vast text available to the West. Theology written through ceremony dominates these pages from start to finish. It is long, dense, and rich in old lore.
sbe-05-pahlavi-texts-1:
E. W. West Englished the Pahlavi Texts for Sacred Books of the East in 1880. Volume Five of Max Müller's great series holds Part One here. Middle Persian writings of the Zoroastrian faith fill this volume.

The Bundahishn leads, with its tale of creation and the world's frame. Other texts treat the soul, good and evil, and the end of days. West's notes guide readers through a hard, little-known tongue with care. Müller's series opened the Persian scriptures to wide English reading. This part pairs with Part Two later in the same grand series of translations. Together they give the Pahlavi books a firm English home.
scott-journal-vol-1:
Walter Scott began his journal in 1825, just as the publishing crash that ruined him approached. Volume One, published in 1890, covers the first years of the record. Scott was then the most beloved novelist in Britain, and a secret partner in a failing firm.

He writes of the crash, his resolve to pay every debt by his pen, and the grind of writing for money. Fame, friends, and Abbotsford fill the brighter pages. The journal is frank about age, illness, and sorrow. Readers meet the man behind the Waverley novels, working himself toward the grave with honor.
scott-last-expedition-vol-1:
Scott's Last Expedition, published in 1913, prints the journals of Captain Robert Falcon Scott from the Terra Nova expedition. Sir Clements Markham, the expedition's patron, wrote the preface. Scott's own diary entries run up to the last days of his life on the ice.

The journals follow the voyage south, the base at Cape Evans, and the sledge trips that laid the depots. Then comes the polar march itself: the Pole reached a month after Amundsen, and the slow death of the party on the way back. Scott's final entries, written as he lay dying, are among the most famous pages in exploration.
seneca-tragedies-miller-loeb-1917-vol-1:
Frank Justus Miller translated Seneca's tragedies for the Loeb series, first printed in 1917. Volume one holds Hercules Furens, the Troades, Medea, Hippolytus, and Oedipus. Seneca, tutor and adviser to Nero, wrote closet dramas of passion, revenge, and stoic endurance that later ages staged with delight.

His Medea outdoes Euripides in fury, and his Oedipus darkens Sophocles with omens and ghosts. Renaissance and Elizabethan playwrights fed on these plays for their ghosts, tyrants, and long speeches. Shakespeare's generation knew Seneca as the model of tragedy in Latin. Miller's facing-text edition made the whole corpus handy in English. Volume two completes the ten plays.
shareholders-deep-waters-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs opens this Deep Waters tale with a night-watchman musing on sailors ashore. A sailorman at sea is safe, like a fish in water, the watchman holds. Ashore, trouble finds him: one man he knew kept marrying in port and faced six wives in court at once.

Money burns sailors worst of all, the watchman warns. Crowds eye a paid-off man's purse until it vanishes. One chap hid sixteen pounds so well he never found them again. The watchman hid two pounds the day before his wife's spring cleaning, with like luck. Jacobs frames a comic warning in dockside speech.
sheridan-memoirs-vol-1:
Philip Sheridan published the first volume of his memoirs in 1888, the year of his death. Sheridan was the Union's hardest-riding cavalry general. Volume One covers his rise and his great campaign in the Shenandoah Valley.

He recalls West Point, frontier duty in the West, and the war's early battles in Tennessee. In 1864 Grant gave him the Army of the Shenandoah, and his ride to Winchester became legend. Sheridan writes as he fought: fast, blunt, and sure of himself. His account of burning the Valley's barns and mills still stirs argument today. His feud with fellow officers breaks through the formal reporting.
sherman-memoirs-vol-1-part-1:
William Sherman, the Union general, published his memoirs in 1875. Part One of Volume One covers his life before the Civil War's great campaigns. Sherman writes in plain, unvarnished prose, with no patience for glory talk.

He recalls West Point, service in Florida and California, and the gold rush days in San Francisco. Banking failure and a post running a military school in Louisiana follow. When secession came, Sherman saw the war's scale before most men did. This opening part sets up the soldier who would march through Georgia. His bond with Grant, sealed in these years, matters later in the war.
sketches-new-and-old-part-1:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old open in this first part, which prints the whole set's contents at its head. My Watch, Political Economy, and The Jumping Frog lead the list. Journalism in Tennessee and the tales of the bad and good little boys follow close behind.

Niagara, poultry raising, and the McWilliams family's bout with membranous croup fill the early range. Twain looks back at his first literary venture and at being sold in Newark. Part one carries the set's front half of hoaxes, tales, and newspaper fun, in the order the full contents promise.
speeches-on-questions-of-public-policy-v:
James E. Thorold Rogers edited Volume I of John Bright's Speeches on Questions of Public Policy. The motto reads Be Just and Fear Not. This is a second edition. Rogers praises the chosen speeches as models of speaking. Men may reject Bright's view of the public good. They will still grant his clear words. They will grant his skill in setting out an argument. His force of style will win them as well.

Rogers praises Bright's candor above all. Bright states his views with full frankness, he says. Events will push more men toward public affairs. Such men will study speaking as an art. For them, no English book helps more than this one. A close and repeated reading is his advice. Tried by their effect on a crowd, the speeches pass. Tried by the old rules of rhetoric, they pass as well.
spencer-autobiography-vol-1:
Herbert Spencer, the philosopher of evolution, published the first volume of his autobiography in 1904. Spencer coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest' and built a vast system of thought. Volume One covers his youth and the forming of his ideas.

He recalls a Derby childhood, an engineer uncle, and his brief work on the railways. Spencer was mostly self-taught and fiercely independent in mind. The volume traces his first books and the start of his grand plan to explain all nature by evolution. His dry, exact manner matches the system builder readers meet in his philosophy.
st-george-and-st-michael-volume-1: George MacDonald wrote St. George and St. Michael in three volumes, and this is Volume I, printed at London in 1876. The contents open with Dorothy and Richard, then Richard and his father. The witch and a chapter of fools come next, then heads of blame, preparations, and musings. An adventure, love and war, Dorothy's refuge, and Raglan Castle follow, and the list runs through the two marquises and the magician's vault to Dorothy's initiation.
st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-girls-: St. Nicholas, Scribner's picture magazine for girls and boys, conducted by Mary Mapes Dodge, fills Volume V from November 1877 to November 1878. Scribner and Co. of New York printed the volume under an 1878 copyright, at the press of Francis Hart and Co. Its contents open with A Child-Queen by Cecilia Cleveland, at page 1, then Chased by Wolves by George Dudley Lawson. A jingle, verses, Mollie's Boyhood by Sarah E. Chester, and the largest volcano in the world by Sarah Coan follow.
stanley-through-dark-continent-vol-1:
Henry Morton Stanley's Through the Dark Continent tells his 1874 to 1877 expedition across Africa, down the Congo river. This first volume, in the 1899 Newnes edition, covers the start: Zanzibar, the inland march, and the lakes. Stanley had found Livingstone in 1871; now he aimed to settle the map's last great questions.

He circumnavigates Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika, proving their shapes and outlets by boat. Then he commits his party to the Lualaba river, gambling that it is the Congo. The volume ends with the expedition poised above the unknown river. Stanley's driven style, and the expedition's heavy death toll, hang over every page.
statius-mozley-loeb-vol-1:
Publius Papinius Statius, a Neapolitan poet at the court of Domitian, wrote the Thebaid, an epic in twelve books on the war of the Seven against Thebes. J. H. Mozley's Loeb translation opens the poem in this volume, with books one through seven. The Latin text faces his English.

Two brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, agree to share the throne of Thebes by turns, then fall out and raise armies. Statius fills the road to war with omens, feasts, a night raid, and the deaths of young heroes. His verse is rich, swift, and steeped in Virgil. The Thebaid was the great Silver Latin epic, read all through the Middle Ages.
stories-by-american-authors-volume-1:
Volume I of Stories by American Authors, in its 1903 printing, gathers five tales: Who Was She by Bayard Taylor, The Documents in the Case by Brander Matthews and H. C. Bunner, One of the Thirty Pieces by William Henry Bishop, Balacchi Brothers by Rebecca Harding Davis, and An Operation in Money by Albert Webster.

Taylor's opening tale is told by a man pressed by a friend to confess a strange, unhappy love that left him shamed yet glad he can feel shame. The set shows the range of American short fiction of its day, from mystery and money matters to street musicians and secrets kept too long.
stories-by-foreign-authors-german-volume:
German, Volume 1 of Stories by Foreign Authors, presents six tales in English dress. It holds Heyse's The Fury and Lindau's Philosopher's Pendulum. It also holds tales by Sacher-Masoch, Baumbach, and Hoffmann. Zschokke's Adventures of a New-Year's Eve closes the set.

Heyse's Fury, also called L'Arrabbiata, opens at dawn under Vesuvius, where fishing folk along the Sorrento cliffs haul in nets cast the night before and rig their boats for the day. Passion by the sea, music, magic, and strange bargains carry the volume's mix of German story craft.
strabo-geography-hamilton-falconer-vol-1:
Greek geographer Strabo mapped the known world in his Geography, written near the start of the Roman Empire. Hamilton and Falconer translated it for English readers. Volume One holds Books One through Seven.

Strabo covers Spain, Gaul, Britain, Italy, and the northern lands. He mixes maps in words with history, myth, and trade notes. His learning is vast, drawn from many lost writers. Errors sit beside sharp, firsthand-grade reports. The set is the largest geography to survive from the ancient world. This volume opens that atlas for readers who love old places.
strange-stories-chinese-studio-giles-188:
Herbert A. Giles translated Pu Songling's Liaozhai zhiyi as Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio in 1880. Volume one gathers the first half of his pioneering selection. Pu Songling, a Qing dynasty scholar, collected tales of fox spirits, ghosts, dreams, and judges of the dead over a long life of teaching.

In these brief tales the dead visit lovers, foxes take wives, and scholars bargain with spirits. Giles, a British consular officer and sinologist, made Chinese supernatural fiction known in the West. His notes explain customs, beliefs, and wordplay for English readers. The tales mix horror, humor, and tenderness in a few pages each. Volume two completes Giles's selection.
sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-volume-1:
Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, published Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands at Boston in 1854, in two volumes illustrated from designs by Hammatt Billings. Volume I opens the record of her tour through Britain and Europe, made in the first flush of her fame.

Her preface owns the charge before critics make it: everything here is given couleur de rose, rose-colored. Why not, she asks; the book holds the impressions, as they arose, of a most agreeable visit, and could not honestly be otherwise. The letters home report the people, houses, and scenery that delighted her, and the warm welcome that antislavery readers abroad gave the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
sylvia-s-lovers-volume-1:
Volume I of Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers, printed at London in M.DCCC.LXIII, or 1863, opens the three-volume novel. Chapter I introduces Monkshaven, a town on the north-eastern shores of England holding about fifteen thousand people at the time Gaskell wrote.

The contents run from a ship home from Greenland and buying a new cloak to the story of the press-gang and a sailor's funeral. Philip Hepburn is named in the fourth chapter, and later heads promise attraction and repulsion, the specksioneer of the Greenland fleet, a refractory pupil, and visions of the future. The volume ends with perplexities and partnership, having set Sylvia between the whaler who courts her and the cousin who keeps his love quiet.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-1:
John Addington Symonds opened his Renaissance in Italy in 1875 with the despots. Volume 1 paints the tyrants whose courts made the age possible. Visconti and Sforza rule Milan in his vivid, crowded opening book.

Power becomes an art form in the Italian city-states he describes. Courts shine with poets and painters while daggers wait in halls. Symonds writes with a poet's eye for splendor and for blood. He neither hides the cruelty nor dims the era's bright genius. Readers feel why strongmen and great art grew side by side. The volume sets the stage for the whole vast work.
tabqat-i-nasiri-raverty-vol-1:
Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani wrote the Tabakat-i Nasiri in Persian in the thirteenth century. H. G. Raverty put Volume 1 into English in 1881 for modern readers. The chronicle covers the Muslim dynasties of Central Asia and India.

Ghurid kings, early Delhi sultans, and court wars fill the narrative. The Mongol storm gathers at the edge of his world as he writes. Minhaj served at court and saw much of what he records. His voice carries the weight of a witness, not a mere copyist. Scholars treat the work as a prime source for medieval India.
tales-and-novels-volume-07-patronage-par:
Volume VII of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels, in ten volumes with engravings on steel, holds the first part of Patronage, her long novel of professional life. The pages at hand give the title and a contents list of numbered chapters without heads, so the shape must be taken from the volume itself.

Patronage follows the Percy family, whose sons must make their way in law, medicine, the church, and the army, against rivals lifted by interest and connection. Edgeworth's theme, stated across the novel, is the contest between merit left to itself and careers carried by patrons. This first part sets the family, the suitors, and the great man's promised favor in motion, leaving the reckoning to the volume that concludes the tale.
tales-from-the-arabic-payne-1884-vol-1:
John Payne followed his Nights with Tales from the Arabic, and Volume I appeared in 1884 as the companion set. These stories come from the Breslau and Calcutta Arabic editions, tales the main cycle lacked room for. Payne Englished them in the same full, unexpurgated manner that marked his Thousand Nights.

The companion volumes catch the overflow of a story-world too big for one frame. Kings, lovers, and tricksters appear in fresh combinations, with the same narrative relish. Volume I opens a three-volume supplement that completists prize, since it widens the map of Arabic tale-telling beyond the famous nights.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-1:
Charles Maurice de Talleyrand served France under kings, a revolution, and an emperor. The first volume of his memoirs, in Beaufort's translation, covers his youth and rise. Talleyrand wrote late in life, defending his own record.

Volume One moves from his birth and church career into the Revolution and the Directory. It ends amid Napoleon's climb to power, with Talleyrand at his side as foreign minister. The tone is cool, witty, and self-assured throughout. Readers meet the supreme survivor of French politics explaining, in his own words, how he stayed standing. Readers should note he writes to justify choices that many condemned.
targums-etheridge-vol-1:
The Targums are the old Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible, read aloud in synagogues when Hebrew faded from daily speech. J. W. Etheridge's 1862 volume gives the first English rendering of two of them: Onkelos on the Torah, and Jonathan ben Uzziel on the same books. This volume covers Genesis and Exodus.

A targum is more than a translation: it smooths hard verses, adds bits of story, and softens bold pictures of God. Etheridge prints the two versions so readers can follow where each expands the plain text. The result shows how ancient Jews heard and taught their scripture. Scholars still use Etheridge as a first path into the targums.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-1912-vol:
John Sargeaunt translated Terence for the Loeb series in 1912, with the Latin text facing his English. Volume one holds The Lady of Andros, The Self-Tormentor, and The Eunuch. Terence, a former slave from Carthage, became Rome's most polished comic playwright, famed for humane plots and clean Latin.

The Self-Tormentor punishes himself for exiling his son over a love match. The Eunuch, his boldest play, threads disguise and mistaken identity through a soldier's rivalry. Sargeaunt's edition was long the standard English Terence for schools and general readers. The facing Latin lets students test the translation line by line. Volume two completes Terence's six surviving plays.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: No page of George Meredith's novel stands here for volume one. The book is The Adventures of Harry Richmond. A Project Gutenberg wrapper stands in its place. The wrapper names the book and author. It marks the part as number 50 in a Meredith set. It gives file number 4444. A release date of September 2003 is given. The file's maker is named as David Widger.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-1:
Mark Twain, whose real name was Samuel Langhorne Clemens, wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, and this first part carries his preface, signed at Hartford in 1876. Twain says most of the feats in the book really occurred, one or two from his own boyhood.

Huck Finn, he says, is drawn from life, while Tom blends the traits of three boys he knew. The odd beliefs he touches on were common among children and slaves in the West thirty or forty years back. He aims the book at boys and girls, yet hopes adults will read it to recall how they once felt and talked. Readers meet Tom, Aunt Polly, and the whitewashed fence in St. Petersburg.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-1: Contents pages alone open the first volume of George Meredith's The Amazing Marriage, dated 1895. Dame Gossip enters as a chorus and tells of the Countess of Cressett running off with an old buccaneer, helped by postillion Charles Dump. Book One moves through a mountain walk, a natural philosopher, and the lady's letter. Book Two lists Small Causes, The Prisoner of His Word, and Opening Stage of the Honeymoon. Book Three promises fog, gout, and an old seaman. It also promises a kidnapping that does no great harm.
the-armourer-s-prentices-1:
Charlotte M. Yonge aimed this 1889 Macmillan novel, pictured by W. J. Hennessy, at citizen life in early Tudor days, as her preface explains. She drew on Stowe's Survey of London, Loftie's history, and Burton's work on English merchants. Stowe, she says, fully describes how apprentices stood toward their masters.

Yonge confesses one doubt: whether her Edmund Burgess could rightly become a citizen of York after serving his time in London. Evil May Day, she notes, follows Hall's Chronicle closely, though a ballad ascribed to Churchill differs in places. A story-teller, she claims, may follow whichever source suits the tale. Hall also supplies her sermon, the king's sports, and the Field of the Cloth of Gold.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Gilbert Parker's first volume carries the same introduction as the complete romance, in which he refuses to write only of Canada. He had spent seven years on northern tales and feared ending by imitating himself. A trip to Jersey in 1897 gave him a fresh field.

Contents list an invasion, then scenes eleven years after, in France, and in Jersey five years later. That spread of time and place sets up a long romance rather than a single episode. Volume one therefore holds Parker's statement of purpose and the opening movements of a story he planned to range widely, in line with his own conscience and impulse.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-1: Volume three of a New England magazine of history, biography, literature, and state progress was published in Boston in 1885 by the Bay State Monthly Company at 43 Milk Street. Its opening pages list the contents of the whole volume. Entries include Samuel Adams the Patriot, the home of Whittier at Amesbury, John Albion Andrew, and pieces on assessment insurance. Page numbers and illustration counts are given for many items. No article text itself appears in these opening pages.
the-boy-slaves-1:
Captain Mayne Reid opens The Boy Slaves, dated 1865, with a grand address to Africa, which he calls the land of Ethiope. He hails it as the home of the lion, the panther, the elephant, and the great crocodile. Then his tone turns: last and most sad, it is the land of the slave.

Reid warns his readers that doom may sit closer to their own homes than they think. White men by the hundreds, he claims, toil in the far inner lands as slaves of slaves. Two wastes meet there, the desert of sand and the Atlantic, with no line but in thought between them. The shore from Susa to Senegal is dreaded by sailors above all shores.
